THE "VIN•SANTE" AND NON-ALCOHOLIO BEVERAGE
COMPANY LIMITED.

This Company is formed for: the purpose of manufacturing " Vin-Sitnte," and for the purchasing, carrying on, and ex- tending of the business established by Messrs. Morgan, Kemp- star, and Co., of Liverpool, the marnnacturers of the above now celebrated non-alcoholic beverage, and also for tha ma nu• factute of all such well-known aerated waters as soda, potass, seltzer, and lithia, and other mineral waters, in which there Is ample scope for a large and highly profitable business. Messrs. Morgan, Kempster, and Co. have also perfected a series of non-alcoholic natural fruit thampagnes, of a very superior quality, for which there is already a large and increasing demand.

" Fin-Sante" is universally pronounced to be the most .ferfect non-alcoholic beverage yet produced. At the Inter- national Food Exhibition, held at the Agricultural Hall, London, in November last, the only Prize' Medal was awarded to " Fin-Sante " in competition with other well-known aerated beverages. In the other aerated beverages mentioned above it will be suffleient to say that there are only a few manufacturers who have fully developed this brauch of the trade, thus giving the Conapany a wide opportunity for the profitable use of capital in this direction. rln addition to 'nil-Sante" a perfectly non-alcoholic beer has been produced, which has been specially designed to meet the requirements of the working classes in price, taste, and quality. The exclusive right to manufacture and sell this beer and the above-mentioned non-alcoholic natural fruit champagnes is in- cluded in the sale to the Company. The Company also propose to produce new temperance and ton-alcoholic beverages of a superior and high-class quality, which will be supplied at a moderate piles to the public, and so meet the demands of tire large and increasing portion of our population who absta,n from intoxicants—a want which has not been hitherto supplied. , .The purchase money payable to the vendors is Z 20,000, ex- clusive of the plant, fixtures, str,ck in trade, and machinery, which are to be take over by the Company at a valuation. The vendors bind themselves to take up, in part payment of the purchase money, not less than £lO,OOO fully paid up shares in the capital of the Company. The Company has entered into a contract with the eminent lirm of Messrs. Evans, Sons. and Co., wholesale druggists of Liverpool, for selling" Vin-Sante" on highly-favourable terms to the Company, thus sucuring the ramifications of their large connection for the development of the sale of " FM-Sante,' ,Met_ra. Evans, Sons, and Co. under the terms of their contract taktrg the s le agency I r the whole of the Halted Kingdom, an well as India, the British dependencies, and fore! ix countries, where they have already established cunnee- , .tions. • • In connection with Messrs. Evans. Sons. and Co.. the influen- tial firm of Messrs. Crosse and Blackwell, of London, have also undertaken a special agency for the sale of rr Vin-Sant4." The advantage of the arrangements referred to above with firms so wrrll 'known will be apparent, their names being at once a guarantee for the popular excellence of "Fin-Sante. ' while their united means of bringing it within the reach of every class of consumers ore unequalled. The sale of " yin-Sante" alone it is expected will leave very remunerative manufacturing profit on the whole capital of the Company, while the profits on the sale of she other bevenges, as manufactured at present and proposed, will make this one of the most lusmtive and desirable businesses under- taken by a Joint-stock Company. The Company intends to lay down plant capable of producing 3,000 dozen bottles of their various beverages per day. HUE Calculating only 2000, dozen bottles per day at the very mode- rate rate of profit of 6d per dozen net on all productions, will show a total profit of £lB,OOO per annum, which, upon a paid- up eaPita of £50,000, is equal to 30 per cent. The Directors of this Company, therefore, have every confidence in recommend- ing the undertaking to their friends and the public ELS a good, sound, and safe investment; and, with a beverage that has secured a prize Medal for its excellence, in addition to their other productions, they believe that their anticipations will be fully justified by the results. The shares of another Company,." The Zoedone CompanY. Limited," although only about a year in existence, are already quoted on the Stock Exchange at 1# premium, or over a hun- dred per cent above the issue price. The " Fin-Sante Company," possessing as it does a prize medal for the excellence of its production, has every reason to anticipate a similar (if not larger) enhancement in the value of Its Morgan. whose ability in establishing this bush n. The only contrasts entered into by the Company are : (1) A contract dated the 17th day of February 1881 made between Alfred Morgan an rad Richard Med,: f 't of the first part Edward Simpson Samuel! and Herbert Appleyard Maw Of the second part, and Frederick William DAWBGII 011 behalf of the Company of the third part. • (2) A contract dated the 18th day of February, 1881, made between Edward EMI., John James Evans, Edward Evans the younger, and William Paterson Evans of the one part, and the said :Frederick William Davraon on behalf ssf the Company of the other part. The above agreements and copies of the articles of association may be seen ar; the offices of the Solicitors to the Company. Pr.sPectuses and any further information may be obtained from the Brokers, Solicitors, or the Secretary,. at the Registered Offices of the Company. Apt Mations for shares on the forni accompanying prospectus will he received by the Brokers, Bankers, or may be sent to the SeeretarYr at the Registered Offices of the Company, No, 33, Princess-street. Manchester, March 4th, 1881.

At the close of the year 1881 the quinquennial division of profits will take place All persons whose proposals have been accepted and the premiums paid before the 31st Dec -mber, 1881, will participate in the b nus. From the results of th-, operations of the four years of the present quinquennium there seems every reason to believe that very satisfactory bonus will be declared. INDUSTRIAL BRANCH. The premiums actually received during the year in Vais branch are £1,608,849 Es. 7d., as compared with the sum of £1,407,143 10s. 6d. received during 1879, showing an increase of premium receipts of £201,705 18s. Id. The claims of the year amount to £573,837 Is. 9d., while the total amount of claims paid in this branch is £3,148,360. The expenses of conducting the existing business of this branch are now 3r9 per cent upon the premium income, showing a further reduction from those of last year, and being 10 per cant less than the amount provided at the last valuation.

These exptinses are necessarily higher than those in the or- dinary branch, as the premiums are collected weekly, but they are still lese than those of any other similar company transact- ing purely life assurance business.

The rate of the new .b-u-sitTe;e—carges is upwards of one-half per cent less than that of last year, but inasmuch as .specific provision is made for these charges in the first year's premium, and they are defrayed by Raw entrants, forming no charge whatever upon renewals, their incidence is of no practical moment.

The process of reducing the- extension expenses has been continued during the past year. The expenses incurred under this head show a diminution of more than one-half per cent, and the same remarks apply to these as to the new business charges. The organization of this branch is still maintained in s high state of efficiency. The result of the valuation at the end of the year 1876 completely demonstrated the safety arid soundness of the system on which the Company's industrial business is carried on. .

The directors have since that date caused statistical returns of the most minute and exhaustive character relating to the trensactions of this branch to fie compiled. The books contain- ing these returns have been from time to time examined with an anxious desire to introduce all improvemeuts for the benefit of the assured which may with safety and propriety be adopted. The business of the past four years has been attended with the most satisfactory results, and the directors propose. if the , valuation at the close of the year realises their expectations, to introduce such ndditional alterations and improvements as they I consider can ly• 'made with due regard to the stability ,of the canpany. .

_ LOVE'S TORMENTS, Ye happy swains, whose hearts are free From Love's imperial chain, Take warning and be taught by me To avoid th' enchanting pain; Fatal the wolves to trembling flocks, Fierce winds to blossoms prove. To careless seamen, hidden rocks, To human quiet—Love. Fly the fair sex, if bliss you prize— The snake's beneath the flower; Whoever gazed on beauteous eyes And tasted quiet more? How faithless is the lovers' joy How constant is their care The kind with falsehood do destroy. The crud with despair.

LITTLE BY LITTLE. When the new years come and the ord years go, How, little by little, all things grow! All things grow—and all deczty— • Little by little passing away. Little by little on fertile plain, Ripen the harvests of golden grain, Waving and flashing in the sun, When the Summer at last is done. Little by little they ripen so As the new years come and the old years go. Low on the ground an acorn lies; Little by little it mounts to the skies, flhadow and shelter for wandering herds, Home for a hundred singing birds. Little by little the great rocks grew, Long, long ago when the world was new; Slowly ancLailently, stately and free, Cities of coral under the sea Little by little are blinded —while so— The new years come and the old years go. Little by little old tasks are done; So are the crowns of the faithful won, So is heaven in our hearts begun With work and with weeping, with laughter and play. 4'^i Little by little the longest day And the longest life are passing away, Passing without retnrns—while so— The new years come and the old years go.

There is nothing marvellous about curing by laying on hands. Hands laid .on smartly and vigorously have cured

many small boys of badness. Believe nothing against another but on good authority, nor report what may hurt another, unless it be a greater hurt to another to conceal it. What is the difference between a steam bellows and a sledge hammer? Because the one blows a great deal; the other deals a great blow. There are two classes of people in the Christian Church— the ole is made up of those who do the hard work; the other of th)se who sit by the fire and find fault. eays. If you would enjoy your food, labour for it; if you would enjoy your raiment, pay for it before you-wear it; if you would sleep soundly, let a good conscience be your bed- fellow. Small boy: "Coss they ain't got no looking-glasses to put 'em on again by." And in two minutes he passed his plate for a third piece. The earnest people are so few in the world that their very earnestness becomes at once the badge of their nobility, and as men in a crowd instinctively make room for one who seems eager to force his way through it, so mankind every- where opens its ranks to one who rushes zealously towards some object lying beyond him. A: Ptturosz IN LlFE.—Carlyle once asked an Edinburgh student—uho tells the story in the Milwaukee Sentinel— what he was studying for. The youth replied that he had not quite made up his mind. There was a sudden lightning flash of the old Scotchrnan's eye, a sudden pulling down of the shaggy eyebrows, and the stern face grew sterner as he said :—" The man without a purpose is like a ship without a rudder; a waif,a nothing, ano man. Have a purpose tO life if it is only to kill and divide and sell oxen well, but have a purpose; and having it throw such strength of mind and muscle into your work as God has given you." PECOCIOUS GENlUS.—ltalian 11111.8iCal genius seems again to be coming to the front. Cesare Galeotti, a little bey nine years of age, is causing great sensation in Italy by his musical talent. Me is reported to be able to play eighty or ninety of the most elaborate compositions of the highest class. In fact, it is said that upon the single hearing of any melody, or succession of melodies, he can play them off. He has played before the Pope, and also before the Queen of Italy. Her Majesty intends to have the precocious boy educated at the Milan Conservatoire.---Boys Newspaper. Holtz TIES.—If there is any place on earth where endur- ing friendship can flourish, gentle influences descend, and affectionate gratitude be shown, where the simple and pure intercourse of the sexes can bring unrestrained delight, where every inducement can be offered for kindly Offices, for pleasant surprises, for interesting exchanges of thought, for mutual aid, encouragement, and sympathy, for every- thing in fact that binds men and women together in har- mony and happiness, it must be in the society of brothers and sisters, united as they are by natural ties, by common interests, and by daily association THE QUARRYMAN, THE ADDER, AND TEE ROBlN.—There was once a granite-hewer working in a quarry aiDalbeattie, when, hearing the cry of a bird in distress, he-hastened to the spot whence it came, and found a robin in great distress. An adder, 20 inches long, had dragged itself up the quarry, and was thrusting its head over the edge of a Best built in the brushwood, and containing poor robin's unfledged off. spring. She kept flying down upon the adder and dartine- her beak into his forehead. When the man came to the rescue and assisted the bird in killing its tormentor, the little robin perched fearlessly upon his arm and watched with de- light. And when the enemy was dead she alighted upon his lifeless body and pecked with all her vigour. Then she 're- turned to her nest and sang a song of triumph and gratitude. —Newcastle Chronicle. Homo° STORIES.—The following stories are thoroughly illustrative of native character in India :—When the Murrees came down last year, after looting the stations in the Hurnai Pass, they broke into the Cutchi Plain, to try what they could do there. On hearing of this irruption, the Native Political Assistant went out with a few of his men and some Scinde horse. He employed the telegraph to keep Sir R. Sandeman informed as to his movements, and these were his messages :-1. The enemy have come out from their hills. 2. We advance to meet them. 3. We are running away. Here is another --The Commissariat officer at Sibi was being driven wild by the tricks, honest and dishonest, of his agents, so he threatened one of them, a baboo, with a flogging. The baboo, in a dreadful state of mind, at once had recourse to the telegraph, and sent off the following telegram to headquarters, exactly in the verbiage of his usual official letters: "Commissariat officer threatens flog ' both we father and son. Please arrange!" TEE IMPORTANCE OF SYMBOLS.—Not our logical, men- surative faculty, but our imaginative one, is king over us. Even for the basest sensualist, what is sense but the imple- ment of phantasy, the vessel it drinks out of? The under- standing is, indeed, thy window; too clear thou canst not make it ; but phantasy is the eye, with its colour-giving retina, healthy or diseased. Have I not myself known five hundred living soldiers sabred into crows meat for a piecei of glazed cotton which they called their flag, which, ha you sold it at any market cross, would not have brought above threepence? . . . . It is through symbols that man, consciously or unconsciously, lives, works, and has his being. Those ages, moreover, are accounted the noblest which can the best recognise symbolical work and prize it

_ the highest.—Thomas Carlyle. CARLYLE'S REMINISCENCES.—Were these reminiscences of Edward Irving, and nothing else, they would be of absorbing interest, but they bristle with noted names, with fragments of descriptive eloquence and subtle i analyses of character. There s " Barry Cornwall," slightly Donlon-elegant, not unpleasant," with a "fine, genially rugged little face ;" Dr. Parr is there, visible though not -seen, "a ridiculous old fellow whose strength of intellect was mainly gone to self-will and fantasticality." Irving's ancient chief, Chalmers, may be seen and heard, and is gauged, " of infinitely less thoughts" than Irving, but "far more pains in setting them forth ;" "such an intellect," "professing to be educated and yet so ill-read, so ignorant In all that lay beyond the horizon in place or time as I have almost nowhere met with ;" a man, moreover, "capable of much wiring indolence," yet a preacher whose like, 'I sup- pose, efiere will never again be in arty Christian church." The skirt of the long blue silk dressing-gown of " Trismegis- tus" Laplace is felt brushing by at a session of the Insti- tute; the "dreamy smile in the eyes" is marked "with something of pathos in it, and, perhaps, something of con- tempt." Henry Drummond mocks and poses, "a man of elastic, pungent, and decisive nature, but well-nigh cracked by an enormous conceit of himself." "The great Murray," Byron's Murray, is evoked only to be dismissed as a "stu- pider man than whom in look, in speech, in conduct," in re- gard to the publishing merits of "Sartor Resartus, "I imagined I had seldom or never seen." Dozens of vet more "thin celebrities" parade in the pages and vanish,- such as Captain Basil Hall, who invited Carlyle to "go out with him to Dangles, and there do lunars in his name, to go to the Admiralty, testifying what a careful studious captain was, and help to get him promotion, so the little he tch smilinoly told me." "Adam, indeed I" replied a voice in the crowd ; "do not speak of him; he was evicted iron', the Garden of Eden without com- pensation." AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION IN IRELAND.—It is prOPOSed, and the proposal has met with some favour, in the interest of the tenant farmers, that there should be an agricultural reading class formed in every national school in Ireland,for the male adult population exclusively, at which evening in- struction might be given, in order that by this agency the practical and theoretical phases of the studies might be bsneficially amalgamated. There is much to commend such a proposal, and, although there might be some preliminary difficulties in the way of organisation to be surmounted, it is not easy to understand that any would prove insuperable." At the Agricultural Society's meeting at Paris. M. de Haut presented a report on American competition. It dwelt on the almost gratuitous concession of land, the merely nominal taxation, the eleven hours work a dayt the absence of any necessity for manure, and the fattening of cattle from Texas at 7f. per head, the inference drawn being " Caveant aoricolte." A discussion ensued, in which some of the speakers cited Messrs. Pell and Read's report in proof that America was no paradise, but had her drawb3cks and scourges ; that there was no need to despair, and that with tightened taxation and improved methods the Old World could hold out against the New. DUST BATH FOR Fowls.—No plan we have tried is so good for keeping the birds clean and healthy as allowing them a good dust bath. There are various ways of making this, and also different ways of making them take to it. Briefly, it may be said nothing is so good for the purpose as dry, powdery ashes, taken from the ash-pit before they have been wet, and put under a cover of some kind to prevent them from becoming so. One bushel or so of dry ashes will do for a dozen or more fowls dusting in for a considerable length of time, and when a little powdered sulphur is shaken over the heap occasionally, it makes it sweeter and more effective. There is something, too, in the manner of putting down the ashes. We have had dry ashes lying under a dusting shed for a month or so without a bird attempting to take a roll in it, and all for the simple reason that the ashes were spread out level, and not laid in a heap. When the same ashes were thrown up into a round mound, there was a crowd around it in a short time scratching, and before long nothing but an intricate rolling mass 'of hens' tails, wings, heads, and feet could be seen. FARMERS AND THE MALT TAX.—A correspondent, whose statements mould command attention if his name were given, writes •—" I met last week one of the largest, if not the largest, of English maltsters, and was surprised to learn that in his opinion had not the Malt Tax been repealed, barley would have fallen 4s.' per quarter lOwer than it has done. I learned that the main cause for the depreciation in barley

was the immense stock of malt left over from last season, arising, in my informaet's opinion, from the depression in trade. He remarked: We could hardly give malt away at the beginning of the season, and if maltsters had had to pay the tax we should not have been able to find the money to buy as much barley as we did purchase.' Further, he said that less sugar and more malt was being used in brewing, and that at the end Of the year it will be seen that more malt has been used than for many years past. On relating this conversation to one of the largest London brewers, he endorsed the views of the maltster in question, except, as he dryly observed, that he had not found any maltster quite prepared to give malt away."—Mark.lane Express. A letter which appeared in the Shipping and Mercantile Gazette of the 24th ult., from the pen of Captain George Peacock, F.R.G.S., contained the following :—Large deposits of guano, it is reported, have lately been discovered on a group of small islands in the Vermillion Sea, belonging to Mexico; they are called the Loreto Archipelago, lying off the inlet or bay of Mulege, in the 26th deg. of north lati- tilde; they are also called the rocky islets of St. George, and are but little known. Vast flocks of sea birds frequent these islands, and the beds of guano are said to be very extensive, particularly on the islands of Monserate, Catalana, Santa Cruz,. St. Marcos, and Tortuga; but as it rains here occa- sionally the guano cannot be so good as that found on the rainless coast of Tarapaca, now in possession of Chili. The writer went in an open whale-boat for eighty miles along this coast, namely, from Iquique to the mouth of the Loa, and discovered immense barancas (cliffs) of this invaluable manure in incalculable quantities, previously unknown ; and several of these enormous virgin deposits, which he explored and surveyed, remained still intact ; indeed, the amount of guano for upwards of fifty miles on this rainless coast line, without towns or inhabitants, may be safely pro- nounced to be practically inexhaustible, and will, rio doubt, now be closely surveyed by the Chillan authorities, and ar- rangements made for shipping from 1,500 to 2,000 tons a day to all parts of the world. WisiTER WOODLAND.—The trunks of trees vary in lure with the time of the year—not quite in so marked a manner as the change from the green to the brown leaf on their branches, but sufficiently to tone the aspect of the field. The darkness of the winter view is chiefly produced by the black timber, and black sterns and stoles of the mounds, which, though naturally devoid of colour, appear so at a distance. Meadows remain green all the winter through. yet, looking on the fields from any elevation, the green is lost behind the prevailing shadow. This is the more singu- lar because when the green leaves appear the grass seems again to come into sight. The driving rain of Winter moistens the bark of the elms, and the wetter it is the darker it looks. Oak bark becomes of so dull a gray that a little way off it is almost colourless, and across a field or two fades into the general gloom. Ashes, never decided in tint, lose that they possess, and appear yet harder, as if wood and bark contracted, bracing themselves together to face the blows of the wind. Hawthorn stoles and branches, dimly brown at hand, deepen into black afar. Even the reddish bark of the Scotch fir is deadened with drab, and the withered pollards are dull as the discoloured Stream beneath , them. All the dead wood and decaying boughs uncovered by the fallen leaves add their gray to these sad hues. As the draughtsman with innumerable strokes of his pencil shades his sketch, so the countless branches, side by side and intermingled—the scribbling of the hedges—each, however small, more or less dark, together make the blackness of the winter picture. Thus the trunks, the bark and branches— that is, the wood itself apart from foliage—rule as it were the landscape, and from these the eye derives its impres- sion.—The Author of "The Gamekeeper at Home in "Land."

div.head: CANADIAN CHEESE FACTORIES AND CHEESE MAKERS.
div.p: CANADIAN CHEESE FACTORIES AND CHEESE MAKERS.

As in the United States so in Canada, cheese-making has , had more attention than butter-making, more skill and in- vestigation have been applied to it, and cheese is conse- quently ahead of bntter in average quality. It is, however, probable that the climate and soil are better adapted for the former than the latter- a moist, cool climate, and a natural herbage full of delicate and succulent grasses, appear to be best suited for butter-making: still, it is true that in France, for instance, excellent butter is made where the land is almost wholly under arable cultivation, and the cattle are almost entirely fed on artificial grasses, &c.; and again, a hot climate induces excessive respiration in cows as in other animals, and where this is, there is a larger expendi- ture of fat from the tissues, and a smaller supply of it to the milk-glands. Be this as it may, however, the cheese of Canada in many cases is very good, while the butter is namely of more than second-class quality; but it cannot, at the same time, be denied that the present high-quality of the cheese is owing to the adoption of factories some 12 or 15 years ago. The same thing indeed may be said of the United States, whose cheese—some of it of high average quality, while some will rank as first-class anywhere—was of a very in- ferior character before Jesse Williams established the first cheese factory near Rome, in the State of New York. It may be mentioned here that at the late International Dairy Fair in New York, the highest premium was carried off by Canadian cheese. Cheese factories are already numerous in Canada, while creameries, on a correspbnding system for butter-making, are as yet few and far between; and so it follows that cheese is a centralised and butter an isolated manufacture, the one receiving collective and the other in- dividual study and attention. Thus it is that cheese- making is betr understood, alike in its principles and practices, than is the case in the sister industry. . I must, however, not omit to say that I have tasted several samples of butter in Canada that would be hard to beat in Ireland, and harder still in our London dairy shows. The most conveniently-arranged and best-equipped cheese factory I saw in Canada belongs to Mr. Ballantyne, M.P.P.; it is known as the Tavistock Factory, and is situated a few miles from Stratford. The milk received daily, at the time of my visit, was about 17,0001b5. from nearly 1,090 cows, but this was in the latter part of September. Mr. Ballantyne contracts with his patrons to make the cheese for them at lj cent per lb., and thecheese I saw there was of very good quality, well made and carefully cured; the temperature of the curing-room is kept at about 80 deg. for spring cheese, and 75 deg. for summer, and at 65 deg. for rich autumn cheese. The quantity of salt used is 2to 211bs. per I,ooolbs. of milk; the smallest quantity is used when the curd is

driest. . . . Mr. Ballantyne for many years past has paid much atten- tion to the subject of cheese-making, as also have several other prominent dairymen in Ontario, and their united l ibonrs have done much towards raising the cheese of the Dominism in the estimation of buyers in England. Formerly there was great difficulty and uncertainty in making autumn cheese in Ontario; it was liable to be puffy and I I,orons ; and, as the whey was not always got well out of It, the flavour was frequently unpleasinti. This difficulty has 1, heen completely overcome by "ripening" the milk before 1(1:ling the rennet to it. SCIENTIFIC NOTES. India-rubber is now used for veneering house furniture It was formerly used only for piecrust. The great Buddhist tope of Sar 'Nath, near Benares, is falling to ruin, and its decay is too far advanced to permit of repair. All available details regarding it are to be care- fully examined and recorded, the necessary photographs being taken by the executive engineer, archssological divi- sion. The Academy hears that during next year a party of members of the Alpine flub are expected to explore the southern Alps In the Canterbury province, New Zealand. Some of the mountains in the colony attain a considerable height, Mount Cook, the loftiest, which has never yet been scaled; having, it is said, an elevation of between 13,000 and 14,000 feet. The large and valuable collection of antiquities excavated in Cyprus by Major A. di Cesnola, and comprising jewellery, cylinders, glass, ivories, gold and silver coins, terra-cotta statuettes and toys, and many other relics—a gathering known as the Lawrence-Cesnola Collaction—has been offered on loan to the authorities at South Kensington, who will some time or other be able to arrange for its reception. A hitherto unknown Goethe portrait is attracting much attention in Germany. It is a chalk drawing by Gerhard von Kiigelgen, and appears to be the original study for the three oil portraits of Goethe painted by this artist. Those who have seen this drawing declare that it surpasses in beauty and vivacity any other portrait of the great poet. It was taken in 1808. It is about to be reproduced photo- graphically, and will thus be accessible to the multitude. BUILDING ON CLAY:—It is curious that garden walls built on the sloping surface of a clay hill, if parallel With the slope, will stand for years, whilst those built at 'right angles to the slope topple over in six or seven years. Clay, in fact, on the hill-side follows the same law as the ice of the glacier or the lead on a church roof. It swells like a sponge equally in all directions, but it shrinks as it dries only in the direction of gravity. Hence an intermittent downhill movement, and the disruption of ' all walls that cross it, unless their foundation is carried below the level of variation. The last year has been disastrous to houses built

mer's milk kept through the night is not so deadly cold as the autumn's, and 50 is in a more natural condition; its warmth has brought it into that state which produces the best cheese -that is, it has ripened somewhat, because warmth as well as time is necessary to the ripening of any- thing. He declares his belief, further, that the best cheese cannot be made from fresh, warm milk ; because, though it is of course warm enough, and has never been cold, it has not the required age, and so is unripe. Hence he prefers that one-half of the milk he makes cheese from should be twelve hours old, and this being ripe enough in itself, ripens the fresh morning's milk when the two are mixed together. In summer the ripening of the evening's milk is enough for the purpose, but in the cold weather of autumn it is not, so the morning's and evening's milk are warmed up to- gethered to a temperature of 90 deg. or so, and allowed to stand several hours before the rennet is mixed with them for coagulation, and this is done because the autumn's even- ing milk has been too cold to admit of enough if any ripen- ing. As the mass of milk stand! at the temperature named, it ripens, and the difficulty previously so common disap- pears, the autumn cheese having all the warmth and mel- lowness of character of the summer cheese, and it is not liable to be injured bv the excessive heat of the summer climate • this autnran cheese, in fact, take it for all in all, Is probably the best of the season, whereas it was formerly, it many cases, the worst., The grand principles of the Cheddar system of cheese- by the way, is probably the best system the world knows—consists in the ripening which the curd gets after separating it from the whey, and before salting and pressing it. This ripening comes of keeping the curd warm, and exposing it to the air. But even in the Chad dar system it is well-known that autumn cheese does not mature like that of summer, and this Mr. Ballantyne de- clares is owing to the evening's milk of autumn not having a chance to ripen like that of summer. I was pleased to find that Professor Arnold, an able exponent of the Ched- dar system, has done much good in Canada in teaching dairymen how to manage floating-curds—that is, by ex- posing them longer in the vat, and by developing more. acidity to checkmate the taint which is common to floating- curds. The milk is generally delivered once a day to the Canadian factories, mod the farmers, under pain of having their milk rejected, are required to take proper care of the evening's milk, and to deliver it in good condition at the factory. CALDERON DE LA BARce.—The Royal Spanish Legation in London notifies that the Royal Spanish Academy has decided to open a poetical competition in London to cele- brate the forthcoming second centenary of the immortal poet Calderon de la Barca. Writers are invited to contd.- Ibute poetical compositions in honour of Calderon in the lEnglish languagp, the form of which shall be lyrical or nar- rative verse, the length, character, and metre being left to the choice of the authors. The compositions must be sub- mitted on or before the Bth of April next to a tribunal, on which, at the request of the Spanish Minister, the following gentlemen have kindly consented to act as jurors :—The Right Hon. and Most Reverend Richard Chenevix Trench, Archbishop of Dublin, falace, Dublin; his Excellency the Hon. James Russell Lowell, Minister of the United States of America; 10, Lowndes-square, London, S.W. ; and the Right Hon. Lord Houghton, 7, Clifford-street, London, W. The compositions having been examined by the above-named jury, and the author of the best (if of sufficient merit) being designated as a candidate for the prize to be aWarded by the Royal Spanish Academy, his Majesty's Minister in London will deliver in due time to the successful competitor : —(1) A gold medal of not less than 100 grams in weight, with the effigy of Calderon and the emblem of the Spanish Academy. (2) A diploma issued by the Academy certifying to the poet's triumph. (3) Five hundred of the 1,000 copies which the Academy will have printed at its own expense, the Academy undertaking to distribute gratuitously the re- maining 500 copies of the composition, the copyright of which will, however, remain, the property of the author. The compositions are to be sent to any of the above-named jurors or to the Spanish Minister in London, 12, Queens- gate-place; on or before the above-mentioned date. Further particulars, if required, will be supplied on application at the office of the Spanish Legation, between the hours of two and four. THE DEEPEST COAL PIT IN BRITAIN.—After six years of patient toil, involving a deeper descent into the bowels of the earth than has yet been reached by any similar effort, the Ashton Moss Colliery Company have, within the past few days achieved the object, namely, the proving of valuable coal beds upon an unworked part of Ashton Moss. In 1874 the company commenced sinking operations with the view of finding the Four-feet mine which was being worked in other parts of the coalfield. Al a depth of 450 yards the mine was proved, and several headings were driven by way of testing the bed, which, however, was found to be not of sufficient thickness to be workable. The proprietors did not build their hopes upon this mine, and, nothing . . .

There has been a considerable increase in the redemption of rent charge during the past two years, owing to the additional powers contained in the Act of 41 and 42 Vic., c 42. Under this Act, any rent charge not exceeding 20s. may be redeemed at twenty-five years' purchase, without a prior division of the land on which it is charged. It also enables the parties, where all concur, to redeem larger sums at not less than twenty-five years' purchase. We have made 5,676 altered apportionments, and confirmed 4,947, and of these 153 have been received and 131 confirmed during the year 1880. We have received 3,964 applications for the redemption of rent charge, and have completed 3,294 of such redemptions; and of these 423 were received and 360 completed during the year 1880. At the close of 1880 we had confirmed 15,264 distinct mergers of tithes or rent charges.

A country boy was riding a horse to one of the English fairs for sale, when he was accosted by a sprig of a dealer, who called out, in a consequential tone, "Why, Jack, the horse you're riding is badly—look what a white face he's gettani" "Hey?' said the boy, breaking off whistling, "an' yo'd have a white face, too, if yo'd looked through a halter ax long az he hez." ANAGRAMS.—The following is an extract from an old Northampton Mercury of April, 1823, which may interest your readers :—" The writing of anagrams, trivial as this recreation may appear, was once the favourite amusement of men of learning and ingenuity, and has found an advo- cate in one of the most learned of our English writers, Camden, who in hi a 'Remains' has bequeathed to the world a treatise on the curious subject. Among modern nations, the French appear to have cultivated this species of wit, which Camden says' they exceedingly admire and celebrate for the deep and far-fetched antiquity and mystical meaning thereof.' Of the success of the Romans in this art we have no example. Camden furnishes only a single instance of English anagrammatism, which is on James I.:— Charles James Stuart ' Claims Arthur's seat. And this, says the author, gravely shows the king's un- doubted rightful claim to the monarch of Britain, as succes- sor to the valorous King Arthur. It was in the reigns of Elizabeth, James, and Charles I. that this description of wit, together with the study of rebuses and illusions, was in the highest repute. A happy anagram on a persons name might have a moral effect on the feelings, as there is reason to believe that certain celebrated names have had some in- fluence on the moral character. When one Martha Nichol- son was found out to be Soon calm in heart,' the anagram, in becoming familiar to her, might afford an opportune ad- monition. Perhaps the happiest anagram of this sort was that produced on Lady Eleanor Davies, the wife of the cele- brated Sir John Davies, the poet. She was the Cassandra of the age, and several of her predictions encouraged her to conceive she was a prophetess. As her prophecies in the troubled times of Charles I. were usually against the Go- vernment, she was at length brought into the High Court of Commission. The prophetess was not a little mad, and fancied the spirit of Daniel was in her from an anagram she had formed of her name:— Eleanor Davies Reveal 0 Daniel. The anagram had an 'l' too much and an a' too short, but the play was sufficient to satisfy her inspirations. The Court attempted to expel the spirit from the lady, and the bishops reasoned the point with her upon the ground of Scripture, but to no purpose. She poised text against text, until one of the Deans of Arches, says Lleylin, shot her through with an arrow borrowed from her own quiver.' Taking up a pen, he hit upon this excellent anagram:— Dame Eleanor Davies Never so mad a ladle. This happy fancy provoked the solemn Court to laughter, and threw Cassandra into the utmost dejection of spirits. The consummation of all this labour, perseverance, and expense was witnessed last Satur- day, when, just Ax years after the ground was first broken, the Workers touched the Great Mine, a seam of coal Oft. thick, and lying at a depth of 895 yards from the surface, or 897 yards including the seam itself. At a depth of 950 yards lies the Roger Mine, 4f I. thick, and below this are sup- posed to exist several workable esams of coal, including the Black Mine and the Cannel Mine, both of which are got at Ashton. The coal is a house-fire coal, with coking properties, and is most valuable for position—being so near the largecentres of population—available quantity, and excellence. The field that can be worked by the company is about 2,000 acres in ex- tent, extending from Guide Bridge to Droylsden on one side, and on the other from Fairfield to Ashton. A second shaft is now being sunk, being, indeed, but 200 yards short of the first shaft, and when working operations have fairly begun —which is expected to be in six months—the mines are cal- culated to yield from 1,500 to 2,000 tons per day, . and plant is being put down with that view. In the sinking opera- tions the miners have encountered no fewer than 60 seams or strata of coal, cannel, or shale, varying from three inches to more than two feet in thickness, but none, until now, of a workable character. The temperature taken at a depth of 880 yards was 78 degrees Fahr. The Great Mine—the one, that is, which has just been proved—has been worked from the outcrop to within a distance of 2,000 yards at the Lord's Field Colliery and about 1,000 yards by the Dukin- field Coal and Cannel Company,. fair rise and dip." The first-named pit pierces the seam vertically at a depth of 130 yards, and the Chappel and Dewsnap pits of the latter corn- patsy strike it at about 250 yards. In comparison with other pits, the Ashton Moss pit, as already stated, is the deepest in England. The sinkings and borings have pene- trated to a depth of 1,050 yards; the siosings alone have reached 895 yards, and this will soon be increased to 950 yards. The Astley Deep Pit, at Dukinfie.d, is about 686 yards deep, whilst the Rose Bridge Pit, at Wigan, and the Moss Pit, situated in the same locality—which have hither- to been reckoned the deepest in the country—extend to a depth of about 820 yards.

''klrlfriqESTY'S FRIME MINISTERS. ' LORD DERBY. When the Liberal Government came to grief in 1866, the question at once arose, to use the words of Thomas Carlyle, "Who shall be Premier, and take in hand the rudder of government, otherwise called the spigot of taxaticest" But, when it was known that Lord Derby had been summoned to the Palace, it was generally thought that, with a following of less than 300 in the House of Commons, he would never undertake to govern the country, and that to make such an attempt would only be an impudent defiance alike of popu- lar feeling and constitutional practice. It was just possible that he might become again, what the Spectator happily called him, "a long vacation Minister," and then, when the next Session arrived, could, on the first adverse vote, do as he had done twice before—dissolve Parliament, and take his chance. But by so doing, while his lordship might se- cure a nine months' lease of power, he would also secure a damaged reputation, for such proceedings could only con- vert our Parliamentary system into a mere farce. But the "Rupert of debate" was not a statesman troubled by many scruples, as was clearly shown. by the contrast between his 'speech at the opening of the ftevious Session and his subse- quent conduct. With the blood of the Stanleys, in his veins, he had before accepted a position the most humiliat- ing, and this he was prepared to do again, if, by so doing, he could "dish the Whigs." It was his lordshipai misfortune, however, to be in office without being in power. Be and his party had been able, by a series of discreditable intrigues, which were all the more unworthy because of the personal animus by which they had been inspired, to defeat a moderate measure of re- form, and overthrow a Ministry which had conducted the business of the different departments of Government with singular ability, and whose one offence was that it was too honest in its attachment to the cause of the people. But it was one thing to filch a Parliamentary majority, and another te reverse the current of popular opinion, and the Tory leaders soon became conscious of this. From the first they knew that the country was decidedly against them, and that, if they would retain for a lengthened period their posi- tion to the right of the Speaker, they mast at once prove their relationship to my Lord Turnabout and Mr. Anything, and that other pliable gentleman whose grandfather was a waterman looking in one direction and rowing another. Accordingly, when her Majesty, in that "clear, silvery voice," with we are given to understand by the newspapers the Speech from the Throne is always delivered, read the "Queen's Speech." Her Ministers caused her to utter the ' following words:—" Your attention will again be called to the state of the Representation of the People in Parliament, and I trust that your deliberations, conducted in the spirit of moderation and mutual forbearance, may lead to the adop- tion of measures which, without unduly disturbing the balance of political power, shall fullY extend the elective franchise.' In accordance with this Royal intimation, the Chancellor of the Exchequer introduced the question of Parliamentary Reform by submitting a series of resolutions which he re- quested the House of Commons to pass as a prelude to its action on Reform. Mr. Disraeli's speech on this occasion was exceedingly elaborate, but it fell short in the essential point of convincing his hearers, and this unique attempt on the part of this adroit and ingenious tactician to shift the responsibility of initiation from the shoulders of the Govern- ment did not meet with general approval. "Why," asked Mr. Robert Lowe—that grim prophet of the white head and thought-burdened brow—" Why should the Government be relieved of the liability to be driven from office on the ques- tion of Parliamentary Reform which other Governments have always accepted? Why should they have the mark of Vain put on them, so that no man could kill them ?" Finding that the proposed resolutions would not carry, Mr. Disraeli abandoned them, and they were accordingly thrown into the Parliamentary waste basket. Having abandoned his resolutions, Mr. Disraeli proceeded to inform the House what would be the main provisions of the Bill which he intended to propose. No debate took place on these provisions. Mr. Gladstone made a few remarks, but theywere by no means of hostile import. The Liberal organs of opinion throughout the country made every allowance for the difficulty of the Ministerial situation, and, so far as appearances went, no Government, in face of a powerful Opposition, had ever more cause to congratulate itself on the way in which its policy was received. But Ministers again lost heart, or rather it turned out that they had too much heart for one section of their supporters. Deserted by three of their most valuable administrators, they abandoned the plan which Mr. Disraeli had laid before the House—a plan which has been facetiously called "The Ten Minutes' Bill." The conduct of the Opposition here appeared to advan- tage. Their patience seemed inexhaustible. Like a father teaching his boy to ride, and encouraging him after every failure to try again, so the Leader of the Opposition, after every confessed blander and bungle of the Ministry, ex- horted them to take heart and make another attempt. For the third time, therefore, Mr. Disraeli went down to the House with a new Reform scheme and laid it upon the table. But it soon became evident that it did not meet with the approval of the House. For its complication it de- mended simplicity—for its ambiguity plainness. No dual voting, no fancy franchises, nothing "new-fangled ;" a bold extension of the suffrage in boroughs and counties, a lodger franchise, and a comprehensive distribution of seats—such were the features which the House demanded in a Reform Bill. And such demands the author of the bill was prepared to grant rather than experience the "hell of failure" 'once more. Accordingly, amendment after amendment was ac- cepted, to the utter bewilderment of his followers. The dual vote which was intended as a sop to the Conservatives, he ridiculed as "the idea of a stray philosopher." The lodger franchise he conceded without any resistance. In- deed, he acknowledged that this franchise was a child of his oar and he held out his hand to it as gracefully as the Marquis of Menmouth did to his grandson Coningsby. Mr. Ayrton moved that the provision for two years' resi- dence should be altered and the term be reduced by one- half, and it was carried by 278 against 197. At length, after twenty-six divisions in a long series of debates spread- ing over a period of seventeen weeks, the bill was read a third time and passed. The bill, after some slight modification, was adopted by the House of Lords, Lord Derby declaring in his speech closing the debate that it was a great experiment, and that they were about to take ." a leap in the dark." But, in our judgment, no event of equal importance had taken place in the political world of Great Britain since the passing of the Reform Bill of 1832. We go farther, and declare that the importance of the Reform Bill of '32 itself will be esti- mated by the historian only from its relation to this far more deeply based, comprehensive, and thorough measure. The Conservative Government, however, deserve little credit for this measure. They succeeded in 'giving birth to it only by the abandonment of a series of positions which they at one time treated as not to be surrendered, and by the aid of the Party which they bad treated with virulence and scorn. A letter addressed by Earl Russell to the Hon. Chichester Forteseue upon the state of Ireland presents the relation of the different parties to the Reform Bill so clearly that we cannot refrain from making one quotation there- from. "We are fated," fay s his lordship, "to show the way of Reform to Tory Ministers. So it has been with Catholic Emancipation, with the Corn Laws, with the Reform Act of 1867. For fifteen years we preached in vain that the ad- mission of the working classes to the frane'

Lord Derby evidently felt that he "served his owe Vier' ation" by endeavouring to thwart its most cherished desires. Rising in his wrath before the democratic deltu,fe that was rising higher and higher, he was heard to exclaim, " to shalt shalt thou come, but no further." But his oppeeiti,°° was as vain and impotent as was that of Canute to the 111; rushing tide. There are those who, perceiving the value 01 a constitutional opposition, are blind to the eVO of indee finitely delaying, if not of finally preventing, Ineasgres which the public interest demands. No one saw this more clearly than Lord Derby 1113 orl to 1834, and his name will ever be associated with the Bee- form Act of 1832, the Emancipation Act of 18339 ".1, Charch Temporalities Act, and the National Board of cation in Ireland. div.head: TICHBORNE APPEAL.
div.p: THE TICHBORNE APPEAL.

---- -- On the confiusion of the arguments for the appellant, I on Friday, the Lord Chancellor and the other learned lords, without calling en the counsel for the Crown, gave judg- ment dismissing the appeal, thus affirming the judgment of the court below. As their lordships are the final tribunal, the Claimant will undergo the remainder of his sentence of fourteen years, unless be receives the Royal pardon. THE ANNEXATION OF THE TRANSVAAL. A meeting of the Transvaal Independent Committee was held at the Westminster Palace Hotel, on Friday afternoon, which was attended by several members of Parliament. Dr. Rare-Blind gave a list of the names of distinguished per- sonages in France, Germany, Austria, and Italy who had signed the protest addressed to Mr. John Bright against the annexation of the Transvaal. It was resolved that a de- putation on the subject should wait upon the Premier at an early date, and it was also determined to increase all efforts in the cause.

in in general terms his intention to uphold the glory of the empire as it had been upheld by Peter,Catherine, Alexander 1., and Nicholas I. He at the same time summoned General Rudiger from Warsaw, and conferred upon him i the com- mand of the Imperial Guards, until then held by himself; renewed the powers of his plenipotentiaries at Vienna, and through them announced his adherence to the declarations made by Prince Gortschakoft on behalf of his late father. On the return of peace, one of the first steps taken by Alexander •IL in the direction of reform was the reduction of the army to the lowest limits compatible with the safety and dignity of the empire. Vigorous efforts were made to place the national finances on a firmer basis, and to promote commercial prosperity. But the greatest reform of all was his emancipation of 23,000,000 human beings from the bondage of serfdom, and an Imperial ukase pro- claimed the liberation ef the serfs, on certain conditions, March 3, 1861. A period of two years was assigned for the settlement of terms, with regard to the quantity of land to be ceded, and the rent, labour, or purchase-money,to be paid for it. In February, 1864, the same boon was conferred upon the Polish serfs, with a view to weaken the influence of the Polish nobility, who owned the greater part of the land, and were consequently all-powerfal. Whether this re- form will have any effect in inducing the Poles to submit quietly to Russian rule remains to be seen. At present theil• national spirit seems crushed by the total failure of their late attempt to achieve independence. As regards educa- tion, great efforts are being made by the Emperor to place the State colleges on a level with the best educational in- stitutions in Europe. A still more notable reform, however, is the inauguration of elective representative assemblies in the provinces. The first of these met in 1865, and it was anticipated that this tentative measure would pave the way for the introduction of a National Representative Assembly. The principal war entered into of late years by 'Russia was that undertaken in Turkestan, against the Arneer of Bok- hare, In 868.—After a resistance of a year and a half, the Ameer fas conquered, his army dispersed, and the city of Samarcand occupied by the Russian troops May, 1868. In March, 1867, the Czar sold the whole of Russian America to the United States for £1,400,000. While Paris was being besieged by the Germans, the Czar declared that he no longer considered himself bound by those provisions of the Treaty of 1856 which Nited his tights in the Black Sea. This led to the conference held in London at the commence- ment of the year 1871, when the parties to the treaty con- sented te its modification in compliatice with the wishes of the Czar. It has been the constant policy of the present Czar to strengthen the influence of the 'church of which he is the head. The result has been a' persecution of all other religious bodies,and especially of the Catholic Church, the bishops of that communion having been forbidden to hold any communication with the Holy See.

div.head: SWEARING ALLEGIANCE TO THE NEW CZAR.
div.p: SWEARING ALLEGIANCE TO THE NEW CZAR.

BT. PETERSBURG, TUESDAY.—The Emperor Alexander, in speaking to some persons who were separately received by his Majesty, said that he ascended the throne under painful circumstances, but that he confidently relied upon the honest co-operation of all patriots. He would endeavour to merit the whole of the love of Russia in the same degree as his father had possessed it. The traditional ceremony of taking the oath of allegiance to the new Emperor Alexander HI. was held in the Winter Palace at one o'clock yesterday after- noon. Following the order prescribed for such occasions, the procession passed through the different salocns of the palace to the chapel. On reaching the lucolar Saloon, where a large number of generals of the army and officers of all arms were assembled, the Emperor was at first scarcely able to restrain his tears, but finally mastering his emotion, his Majesty addressed those present in a firm voles, expressing his warm thanks for the heartfelt sympathy manifested for the loss of his father. The Czar called upon all present to keep the dead Emperor in faithful memory; and to preserve the same fidelity towards himself. At the close of tke address there was perfect silence for some moments, the stillness being only interrupted by the weeping of many present Then, however, enthusiastic hurrahs broke forth, and were again and again r newed until the chapel was reached. The Emperor, whose strong grief hardly allowed him to speak, addressed the assembled members of the Council of the Empire and the Ministers, who, together with the other high dignitaries, took the oath of allegiance. The procession after- wards returned in the same order in which it started. To- day and yecterday the military took the oath to the colours. The streets continue to-day to be greatly thronged, and the people maintain the same quiet and symp.thetic demeanour as yesterday—only one feeling—tinit of grief and pain for the immense loss sustained by the Empire, and abhorence of the act which caused it, are manifested by all classes with- out distinction.
ALLEGED DESIGN ON THE LIFE OF ALEXANDER HI.

Eight more arrests were made in Sc. Petereburg on Wed- nesday, and the authorities believe they have a clue to a plot to taketbedife of the new Czar.' Sappers were en- gaged in searching for a mine which it is alleged has been laid near to the residence of the Emperor. A large crowd collected at the scene and there was much excitement, The Emperor yesterday promulgated a decree granting privileges to persons deported to Siberia, subject to the approval of the Minister of the Interior. In consequence of the additional arrests and new discoveries the trial of the assassin Run- koff has been postponed. It is stated that there was quite an outburst of revolutionary activity in St. Petersburg just on' the eve of the assassination, and the authorities made some important arrests, but not in time to prevent the out- rage. On Tuesday a proclamation was posted up outside the University stating that the assassination was the work of the Executive Committee, and that their work would go on. It was torn down, but another took its place in an hour. There is a report that Count Melikoff on Tuesday gave in his resignation as Minister of the Interior, but that the Emperor absolutely refused it. The Czar has already' sent a special letter to the Eteperor William assuring him that Russia's old friendly feeling towards Germany 'would be by no means changed. At Berlin the news of the outrage has had the effect of in- creasing the severity with which the Socialist law is ap- plied, and a numbenof suspected persons have been expelled the city and its suburbs. An official report states that the anarchic element in Germany, though now unseen, is really more vital and 'vigorous after a lapse of two years than when the law for 'exterminating it was passed. Secret groups and clubs have been formed, a secret Socialist printing office has, been discovered and closed, and regicide is held up as enn of the best means of bringing to pass the pocial revolution. The organ of Prince Bismarck expresses a hope that the mew Monarch may succeed in ridding the Rus.tian people of the pestilential breath of a criminal pro- paganda, which, like an abortion of the modern Zeitgeist, threatens to annihilate all society. Resolutions applauding the assassination have been adopted at a meeting of the New York Socialists, at which speeches of incendiary character were delivered by English, Russian, and German Socialists.

9"44...A TRANSVAAL WAR. PROLONG-ATION OF THE ARMISTICE. NEWCASTLE, Monday —A body of 1,000 farmers from the Orange Free State are stated to have left to join the Boers in the Transvaal. Reports are current that Miller's Pass has been occupied by a Free State contingent. Sir Evelyn Wood , has left here for Mount Prospect. It is rumoured that the armistice with the Boers has been pro- longed. A telegram from Durban states that in tho absence of Erokger, the Boer leader, the armistice has been prolor.ged for four days. MOUNT PROSPECT, Monday, 1-5 p.m; —Lady Colley, accompanied by Mrs. Montague, reached the camp soon after 11, and visited Sir George's grave. She will return tomorrow. Sir Evelyn Wood will not force on fighting!, but if the Boers' demands are still such as the British Govern- ment will not accede to co other course will be open to him. Major Clarke has arrived' here, and takes the post of military secretary. Little hope. rays the Central News, is now entertained in Government circles of a renewal of hostilities with the Boers being averted. It is feared that nothing will come of the negotiations, and that no other course will be left but to re- sume the contest. ` A report from Durban states that the Boers insist on noth- ing short of the annulmeet of Sir T. Shepstone's proclama- tion, and entire freedom from British interferences, Nego- tiations are still pending. A telegram from Fort Amiel to the Standard states that the general opinion is that the Beers have decided to make their Sandssion. In a letter addressed to President Brand by Vice 'President Kruger on behalf of the Triumvirate of Boers, Mr. Kruger complains of the treatmeut the Boers have received, but says he still holds to the offer of the 29th January of a protectorate of the Queen over the Transvaal.
