MR. BRADLATIGH AND THE OITIL—Mr. Bradlaugh, at the time for presenting petitions, rose with a bundle of papers In his band, and was about to announce their purport, when Mr. GORST interposed on a point of order, and asked whether Mr. Bradlaugh's seat bad not been declared vacant on the decision of a mitt of law, and whether be was any harmer entitled to take part in the proceedings of the House. Mr. I Gorst intimated that he would have no objection to have the point referred to a Select Committee.—The ArroratEY- GENERAL said it was the right of every subject that pend- ing an appeal a man was entitled to retain his original position and status.—Sir JOHN HOLLER said the question was whether, when a court of competent jurisdiction had adjudged that Mr. Bradlaugh was not a member of the House, the House ought not to declare the seat vacant, it least pending the issue of an appeal. He suggested that Mr. Bradlaugh should not exercise the rights and privileges of a member of the House.—Mr. LABOUCHFRE said he had been Raked by his colleague to state that in- structions had been given for an immediate appeal. On his own part he protested against the proposal to deprive Northampton of half its representation in that House, in accordance with the decision of a court of first instance. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL said the appeal might be de- layed for twelve months, and all the time Mr. Bradlaugh I might be voting.—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE now inter- posed, and suggested that the point of order should be at once settled without further debating the subiect.—Mr. BRADLAUGH, who had before risen, now being called upon by the Speaker, statid that he had given notice of appeal, and that the judge had stayed execution, anu, as any or- dinary law book would have informed Lord Randolph Churchill be was bound to prosecute the appeal within 21 days.—On the point of ordeethe SPEANER said the matter was one for the determination of the House, and until the House had determined otherwise he should feel bound to look upon the hon. member for Northampton as duly filling his seat. It was therefore his duty, to call upon him to proceed With the presentation of the petitions which be had in charge when interrupted by Mr. Gorst.—Mr. BRADLAUGH then, amid some cheering from below the gangway on the Liberal side, presented 32 petitions against perpetual pen- sions. POSTAGE AND RECETPT STAMPS.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to a question, intimated that he was prepared to meet public convenience by an arrangement that would make the existing penny stamp available either as a receipt or a postage stamp. THE AnatisanCE.—Replying to Mr. Lewis, Mr. GLAD- sTorrE said that after the Cabinet Council on Saturday a communication had been sent to Sir Evelyn Wood autho- rising the extension of the armistice till the 18th. On the question of who proposed the armistice he stated that on March 3 President Brand had appealed to Joubert to meet Sir Evelyn Wood for the purpose of arranging an armistice. On March 5 Sir Evelyn Wood received from Joubert a COM- munication asking him how far he would co•operate in such a movement, and on the elth of March Sir Evelyn Wood wrote to Joubert.

THE ELECTION Comarrsszotegus. —ln reply to Mr. Onslow, the ArrostwEr-GuNgnat, said the reports of the Election Commissioners 'would be in his hands in time for him to take the necessary steps for the commencement of the prosecutions for corrupt practices.—Sir George Camp- bell had placed on the paper a series of questions addressed to the Home Secretary as to the adjournment of the Oxford El ection 'Commission from'Oct:3o to Dec. 22.—Sir Wrrztax HARCOURT observed, amid much laughter, that it was the business of the Commissioners to examine him rather than that he should examine them. Being pressed to say whether the professional engagements of the Commiseioners had anything to do with the arrangement, he answered," I do not know, but I think it very likely." THE UNITED STATES GOVERNMENT AND MICHAEL Borrow. -- To Sir Henry Wolff Sir CHARLES DIME answered that no representations had been made to the Government by the United States Minister on the subject of the arrest of Michael Boyton on the ground that he is an American citizen. THE PROGRESS OF 'BUSINESS.—Mr. DILLWYN nut a series of questions to Mr. Gladst 'lle, obviously founded on the statement made, public in Sir Stafford Northcote's ad- dress to his constituents. Mr. Dillwyn, whose recitation rrf his questions was interrupted by much murmuring from the 'Opposition, was, on resuming his seat, distinctly chal- lenged by Mr. GORST, who put to the Speaker the question whether such questioning was not an evasion of the order of the House, which had decreed that when a vote of urgency was to be taken it s‘‘ould not be prefaced by explanations. —The SPEAKER said he was not in a position to interfere, and Mr. GLADSTONE, whose rising was received with loud cheers from the Liberals, said he would endeavour to keep as closely as possible within the practical 4mits of the ques- tion. It wagnot the ease,,he said, taking the questions in order, that the present demand for urgency had been made from a desire to secure the time from Easter to Whitsuntide for Government legislation. For 20 years the vote for Sup- plementary Estimates had been voted not later than the 21st March, and never so late except in a single instance. It was not usual to postpone the first vote for the coming year after March 31st. The estimates on which supplementary votes were proposed had been framed by the late Government, mad, lastly, it was not till June Ist in last year that the Go- vernment were informed from India that the vote on account of the Afghan war would be over ten millions.—Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE, who had provided himself with a series of pro- positions written out, wanted to know whether if the Lords sat on Wednesday, the 30th, they could not pass the Ways and Means Bill through its last stage, as that it might re- I ceive the Royal assent on the 31st.—Mr. GLADSTONE said that, assuming the House of Commons would be able to read the Bill a third time on Tuesday, the 29th, they had no right to calculate on the House of Lords sitting On a Wed- nesday in•order to meet the •convenience of the House of Commons. But, even if that were so, there was business to be done which would make it impossible to satisfy the re- quirements of the law if the Bill did receive the Royal assent on the 31st. THE PROPOSED NEW WRIT TOR NORTHAMPTON.—Mr. GORST announced that in view of the paramount duty of members not to interfere with the business of Supply he should not proceed with his motion for a new writ for Nortbampton. RR explanation received with incredulous laughter from the Opposition. URGENCY.—Mr. Granaroxn then moved that certain votes for Supply were urgent, and without debate the question was put from the chair by the Speaker.—On a division, the result of which was awaited with evident anxiety, it was found that 290 had voted with Ministers, and 212 against. These figures were received with cheers horn the Opposition, answered by enthusiastic cheering from the Ministerialists. —The SPEAKER said that, it being necessary under the order to affirm a resolution for urgency by a majority of three to one, he could not declare that the "ayes' had it. Th 6 division was taken very closely on party lines. Only one Liberal (Mr. Cowen) voted with the Opposition, and one Conservative (Mr. Newdegate) with the , Ministerialiste. Several of the Irish members, including Mr. A. M. Sullivan. and Mr. Corbet, walked out when the division ,was called. Only eleven of the extreme section of the Home Rulers voted with the Conservatives. ' •

SUPPFT.—In moving that the Speaker leave the chair, Mr. GrAPsrorrn observed that the direction of the business of the House having been placed in the hands of the minority, be acquiesced in the decision. He only hoped that gentlemen in all quarters of the House would show a disposition to e-xpediate proceedings in Committee of Sup- ply. It would be for the Government to reserve the right hereafter to make whatever proposals tbey might think proper for the dignity and honour of the House and for the convenience and necessity of public business. Sir RICHARD CROSS withdrew an amendment to going into Committee of Supply which had a favourable place on the paper. His example was followed by Mr. O'Donnell, and, no other member having an amendment rising, the Speaker at once left the chair. The proceedings in Committee were very quiet and the progress unprecedented. The Conserva- tive Opposition, who had fought so stoutly for the privilege of discussing the Estimates, left the house in a body as soon AS the division was taken, for several hours leaving the money to he voted without, as far as they were concerned, comment or inquiry. By nine o'clock 14 votes were passed and the Irish section reached. Mr. Parnell, who had entered the House an hour earlier, appealed to Mr. Forster not to press the• Constabulary vote and one or two others of special interest to Irish members. This course was agreed to, and the Irish members then retired. In the end the whole of the Supplementary Civil Service votes were passed, with the exception of two or three of the more contentious Irish votes. Progress was reported a few minutes before midnight, and, the remaining orders baring been run through, the House adjourned.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—TtrEmor.

THE ASSASSINATION OF THE EMPEROR OF RUSSIA.— Earl Granville moved an address to Her Majesty expressing the sorrow and indignation of the House at the assassination of the Emperor of all the Russias. and said there might be a difference of opinion amono. Englishmen as to the exact political relations which' ought to exist between Russia and ourselves, but there was absolutely no difference of opinion asto the indignation and deep detes- tation with which they viewed the rment crime. The noble earl added that the Queen had already expressed personally her sentiments of grief and sorrow, and had given the Gov- ernment orders to convey those sentiments in a still more formal way.—Thaarl of BEACONSFIELD seconded the ad- dress, and referred to the late Czar as "the most ehivalrous pricier/ that ever filled the throne of Russia."—The motion having been agreed to, a message of condolence to the Duchess of Edinburgh was moved by Lord Granville, who mentioned the singular and touching circumstance that on the very I morning of the murder the Duchess and her brother con- gratulated one another on the greater sense of security which reigned in their father's bome.—The Dukes of Richmond and Bedford were ordered to attend upon the Duchess Of Edinburgh, and to present to her the message of the House. PEACH PRESERVATION (IRELAND) BILL.—Earl SPENCER moved the second reading of this Bill. Having described its provisions, his lordship said that though it was prema- ture to say how far the coercion measures were likely to 'restore tranquility and peace in Ireland, he might inform the egard people t o were the House that, although the Act already passed had been such a short time in force, considerable improvement was noticeableh e m i n t e n Hamel:it of England was determined to carry a measure for won of awarenrinie thaint the l'an adr.

restoring peace and order in Ireland, the outrages which had created each terror in the country, began to diminish, A return o crime for December, January, and February afforded satisfactory evidence as to the decrease of crime already. h December last year agrarian aims wore 807 in number, including 432 cases of threatening letters. In January there were 439 outrages, Melly:ling 251 theatening letters. In February these outrages had sank to the num- ber of 170, of which 80 were cases of threatening letters. He recommended the present Bill to the House as one that would coerce only a few, while it would restore liberty to the many in Ireland. The Bill was read a second time. .
The report of amendments on the Alkali and Noxious Vapour Bills, and the Rivers Conservancy Bill, were reset
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-TUESDAY.

--„—_ Fnarruz min FERE TRADE—Mr. Maclvan asked whether the delay in the negotiations for a commercial treaty be- tween England and France was attributable to our con- tinued importation of manufactures free of duty, unaccom- panied by stipulations as to reciprocal free trade, and to the consequent difficulty of making it to the interest of France to receive our wares duty free.—Sir C. DILLE : No, sir. My answer must be in the negative. (Cheers.) Mr. MeclvErt gave notice that In consequence of this he will. on an early day, "call attention to the neglect of com- mercial interests on the part of the Government "—(laugh- ter) and will move that cistorns duties ought to be placed on such foreign importations as come into fair competition with the industries of Great Britain and Ireland. (Hear, hear.)

CANDAHAN.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to Sir William Palliser, said he could not nndertake that until the debate on the Candahar question should come on no steps should be taken for the withdrawal of the British gar- rison. •

TIDO ASSASSINATION OF THE CAE.-Mr. GLADSTONE said: I think the House will be unanimously of opiqien that:the assassination of a great sovereign placed upon one of the higlidst thrones upon earth would, even in ordinary circumstances, supply fit occasion to carry to the foot of the British throne expression of our sentiments, and sympathies, end condolence, but in the present instance there are many heightened circumstances which cannot be excluded from our views There is, first, the noble self-forgetfulness, by which it appears that the Emperor, having escaped from the first deadly attack made upon him, was induced to disregard the cautious advice 0 those around him that he should again seek the shelter of his carriage, and to say, "No, it was hisduty to see to the wounded!' (Hear, hear.) Again, I think we cannot but bear in mind that the circumstances of this assassination have reached a pitch of grief and hor- ror perhaps hardly known in the melancholy annals of such deeds. The crime recalls to my mind some sentiments in which the patriarch of all pdets has recorded his feelings upon the fat* of a very ancient sovereign, whose wise and good reign failed to elicit the universal gratitude which ought to have been its consequence and reward.
Let tyrants govern with an iron rod. Oppress. destroy, the scourge of God; Since he, who like a father held his reign. Is soon forgotten, so just and mild, in vain. . . . .

For all knew that. whatever there might be in that great Empire—as doubtless may be found in all communities—to call for criticism and censure in the imperfection of human institutions, none of this was owing to Alexander the Second. (Hear, hear.) If it was, it existed as part of the inheritance he received. The sole labour of his devoted life was with him to improve that inheritance for the bene- fit of his Subjects; and I believe that it is not the language of flattery, nor even the language of mere feeling naturally excused by what has occurred, which leads some to state with confidence that the reign of Alexander the Second In the history of Russia and in the history of Europe and Christian civilisation will ever be regarded as an illustrious and memorable one. (Cheers.) Ile came to the throne when his country was locked in a most deadly struggle with three of the Powers of Europe' two of them amongst the greatest in the world, and he extricated her from that struggle with all the promptitude and with all the honour that the most loyal citizen of this country could have hoped. It was not his fate to pass through a long reign without again seeing his country involved at the close of it in another great and dangerous war, but that great and dan- gerous war was ennobled at least to him and to many who may think with him by the deep conviction of his heart and mind, that it was a war of duty and a war of liberation. If we turned from considerations of peace and war, which must ever awaken in our minds mixed sensations, let us only ask ourselves whether modern times have exhibited a reign more distinguished, more remarkable for the great works of peace- ful legislation which he has bequeathed to the great empire. Perhaps we are none of us aware. I certainly do not pre- tend that I possess myself an accurate or minute knowledge of those works; but then an outline, and even the names of a few of them, ors such as to demonstrate that they were due not only to a sense of high duty and Christian philanthropy, but also to an enlightenel intelligence and a powerful will. It was the happy fate of Alexander the Second by one of the greatest acts ever peacefully accomplished in the annals of civil change to give civil and social freedom to a population of serfs estimated at more than 20 millions of human beings. (Cheers.) It was his happy lot to establish in Russia a system of local government I believe to be thoroughly free, independent, and popular. It was also amongst the triumphs of his reign to introduce into Russia the institution which we fondly think to be specially associated with our own his- tory, the institution known as trial by jury. Nor were these the only acts for which he may claim the favourable judg- ment of the enlightened historian. But my duty is not to enter into a catalogue of those acts. It ie- only to point to a few of the rnore.memorable amongst them, and it is indeed sad that such a man should have met with such a fate. Doubtless there are counsels of Providence behind which it is not for us to scrutinies; which we must believe will tend to all that is wise and good. In the illustration I just now uttered the words were used that the old Sovereign I just now spoke of was "so soon forgot." That will not be the case of Alexander 11. The fond affection of his people will ever cling about his memory, as well as the sympathy and admiration of the world. Under these circumstances it is easy for me to understand in what manner it must be that the Queen, allied as she is with the Emperor of Russia by domestic lies, and thoroughly cognisant of all that has taken place in his reign contemporary with her own, with what feelings she must be impressed by this terrible catas- trophe and therefore I have no more ta do than to invite the douse loyally. earnestly, affectionately, and unani- mously to go to the foot of the Throne and assure her Majesty of the grief and horror with which we contemplate this act, and the sincere and respectful sympathy with which we enter into all feelings which she can and must entertain. (Cheers.) I beg to move that a humble address be presented to her Majesty to convey to her the expression of the indignation and deep concern with which this House Ins heard of the assassination of her Majesty's Imperial relative and ally, his Imperial Majesty the Emperor of All the anasias, and to pray her Majesty that she will be graciously pleased to express to his Imperial Majesty the new Emperor, on the part of her faithful Commons their abhorrence ,of the crime and their sympathy with the Im- perial family of Russia and the Government and people of that country. (Cheers.) . .

Sir S. NjartiscoTE, who was received with cheers, said it must beluite unnecessary for him to add anything to the eloquent language that had just proceeded from the Prime Minister, but he rose in order that there might be no doubt in the minds of those who took note of the proceedings of this House of tjae universal feeling of sympathy and admira- tion for hini *hose life had thus been cut short which animated the people of the country and the members of that House. (Hear? hear.) Throughout the European family them was no member that had felt the thrill of horror more deeply and more sincerely than England. ' (Hear, hear.) They had known, watched, and sympathised with the works so eloquently and truthfully set forth:by the Prime Minister. (Hear, hear.) If there had been moments when political differences might have raised a shade* of jealousy as re- garded the external policy of that great kingdom, never for a mornent bad the hearts of this people ceased to beat with a feeling of sympathy for the personal character and the great legislative labours of the Emperor Alexander the Second. He cordially seconded, and he was sure the House would cordially agree with, the preposition that had been made. (Cheers.) .The vote having been agreed to, Mr. GLADBTONE moved and Sir STAFFORD Noterncom seconded a message of condolence with the Duchess of Edinburgh, which was also agreed to unanimously. PERPETUAL PENSIONS.—Mr BRADLAUGH, in response to an appeal from the Premier, said that though his motion with regard to perpetual pensions was of considerable im- portance, as was shown by 848 petitions, with a quarter of a million signatures, having been presented in favour of it— (hear, hear)—he agreed to postpone ft, but asked the Gov- ernment to give him an early day after Easter when he might bring it in. (Hear, hear.)—All the other hon. meal- hers who had notices on the Paper, or who were in charge bf bills, also gave way, and the House went into Committee of Supply. SuPPLY.—The Irish votes were proceeded with, in ac- cordance with an arrangement made on the previous night. In all there remained eight to be dealt with, the two first, being votes on account of the Local Government Board and Public Works, were passed with brief debate. On the motion for the law charges for criminal Prosecutions a pm- longed conversation arose, Mr. A. M. Sullivan, Mr. T. p. Sullivan, Mr. Biggar, and, in short, all the Irish members present criticising the procedure. A motion was made to reduce the amount by the sum of £3,100, being the fees of barristers and solicitors engaged for the Crown. On a division this was negatived by 153 votes against W. Throughout this discussion and for what followed the at- tendance was very small. The Conservative Opposition wps conspicuously absent, and there were not more than a dozen Irish members in their places. On the Constabulary vote Mr. Parnell, at the close of an hour's discussion, said be would content himself with entering a protest against the practica of keeping a large force of police in Ireland. On a division the vote was passed by 189 against H. This concluded all the votes in the Supplementary Eatimatr, and at a quarter-past 12 progress was reported, and the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. PUBLIC BUSINESS.--Mr. GLADSTONE, answering Sir R. Cross, said he did not see how it would be possible to obtain an interval for the legislative business of the session Juliet's supply was voted on account, as proposed. He added. however, that he was so sensible of the way in which t Holm bad met the exigencies of the Government, that . would propose to take the vote of account for two writ s only; but he Must warn the House that having regard the vote of censure which was imminent with regard Candahar, and the debates on the Irish Land Bill, it might be necessary to propose another vote on account before Whit- =tide.

CANDARIR.—Mr. Graaserenez stated that the Indian Government had rece.ved certain instructions from the Home Government, and be had not the least doubt the Indian Government would, or, he might say, must, make further communication to the Government at home before Candahar could be quitted. (Hear. hear.) SUPPLY: AFGHAN Wen EEPENSES.—The Rouse went into committee of supply, and Mr. GLansrosna proposed a vote of £500,000 as the first instalment of the grant in aid to the Government of India towards the expenses of the Afghan war. He pointed out that the House would here- after have full opportunities of going into any questions connected with the policy of the war or its results. The question was really one of the financial policy to be adopted with respect to India, and the late Parliament had sanctioned ' this policy 'it the instance of the preceding Government by granting the sum of two millions as a loan without interest, and he believed that no one would question the policy and the justice of that proposal. He regretted that he could not give details as to the cost of the War, which he had been most anxious to ao ; but the total cost of the war was ill round numbers about 13 millions—a very much larger amount than was originally estimated or anticipated. He would not now go into that matter, hut under these circumstances the Government had to consider whether the grant in aid already proposed ought not to be increased, and had corns to the decision that it should ask Parliament to in- crease the grant to £5,000,000, to be met partly by remit- ting the payment of the loan of £2,000,000, and partly by taking in ways and means a series of half-yearly grants of half a million, until the sum of £3,000,000 was added to the two millions. It was thought better not to borrow the money, but to take the series of grants in the way proposed, so that each year should pay its share. The right honour- able gentleman made a forcible appeal to the committee to sanction the proposal of the Government as one eminently calculated to conciliate the loyalty and affection of the people of India by showing the deep interest that it took in their welfare, and by its readi- ness • to share in the sacrifices which they had made. Mr. E.• STANHOPE contended that the step which the Govern- ment proposed to take would revolutionise the relations between England and India.—Sir G. CAMPBELL expressed regret that the proposed gift was not to be raised by taxa- tion, so that "gentlemen who paid income-tax, read the Daily Telegraph, and supported the late Government through their organs and otherwise, might have felt the effect of theil cenduct."—Mr. Osistow held that is was "politically immoral for this country to pay arfy portion whatever of the expenses of the Afghan war."—Mr. BRAD- LAUGH thought that the immorality would consist in making the people of the north-western provinces of India pay for a war which was most mischievous to them, and ought never to have been entered into at all Mr. ILLINOWownt argued that the vote would show the in- habitants of India that the great mass of the people of this country were not prepared "to indulge in Imperial fancies on the one hand, while repudiating Imperial obligations on the other."—Lord Hannwerrow, in an able speech, replied to an inquiry made by Sir S. Northcote, and intimated that as the late Government did not consult the Indian Council before commencing the war, the present Government did consider it necessary to consult them on this matter new. that the war was over.—Sir S. Noumea= confined himself to urging Ministers to refrain "for Heaven's sake" from changing the whole relations between the Indian and Im- perial Go arnments, but declined to challenge this particular vote, which was one of an instalment of £500,000 towards the proposed gift —alter some remarks from Mr. FAWCETT, who contended that the proposal was not an act of genero- sity but of justice, the vote was agreed to. MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN BILL. Mr. HOPWOOD moved the second reading of this Bill which was intended to enable married women to enforce claims upon negligent husbands for the maintenance of their children without entering the workhouse and throwing themselves upon the pariah—at present the only way open to them of establish- ing such a responsibility.—Mr. Conartnyr unhesitatingly accepted thetneasure on behalf of the Goverment, remarking that it would only apply to cases where the husband pos- sessed the requisite means, and that to ask that the children should be maintained by him under suchcircnmstances was only a demand of common-sense.—Mr. WARTON opposed the measure on the ground that while there was another bill before Parliament for making women equal to their husbands, the present would make them a great deal better. —Mr. LEWIS moved the rejection of the bill.—Sir. R. Cnoss said he could not conceive it possible that the House would endorse the principle that in the ease of a husband and wife living together, the woman was to be entitled he force a claim upon the man for the maintenance and edu- cation of the children.—The Arronwev-GENEnaa suggested that in Committee the operation of the bill should be limited to cases where the husband was living apart from his wife; but Mr. Hopwood hesitated to distinctly commit himself to this modification.—The adjournment of the de- bate was moved, and the bill was talked out. ROUSE OF LORDS.—Tnuiteney

Blum ADvaxcED.—The Peace Preservation (Ireland) Bill passed through committee without discussion, and was reported to the house. The Alkali and Noxious Vapours Regulation )3111 and the Rivers Conservancy Bill were read a third time.

..... THE GREEK CLAIMS—Lord Strathenden and Campbell called attention to the correspondence on the Greek frontier question, and moved an address to her Majesty for copies of the remaining despatches from the French Government on the differences between Greece and the Ottoman Empire. EARL GRANVILLE said they had not received any additional despatches from the French Government since those already presented to Parliament. The French Government sent two circulars to their representatives here rind elsewhere, and they were publishe4 in the yellow book. The substance cf these circulars would be found in the blue book.

TITRE RENT CIIARGES.—Sir WM. HARCOURT, in reply to Mr. Inderwick, said the Government were not unfavoura- ble to a committee of inquiry into the subject of extraor- dinary tithe rent charges, and also with reference to the ex- pediency of providing general facilities for the redemption of ordinary tithes upon equitable terms; and he invited a conference with him upon the subject. THE BIRMINGHAM LEAGUE AND TIM CARLTON CLUB.— Reply to Mr. D. Onslow and Mr. Labouchere, the Arrormar GENERAL thought it somewhat to be regretted that questions bearing on electioneering contests should be asked in the House of Commons. (Rear, hear.) He had referred to the report of the trial at Evesham before the Election,Judges, and he did not find that their Lordships referred in auy way to Mr. Nuttall as having been guilty of corrupt practices. With regard to the Oxford election, he was unable to see from the reports he had read that the conduct of Mr. Schnadhorst at the Oxford election in any way assisted in contaminating the election. (Hear, hear. He must say, however, so far as his me- mory served him, that a certain person who was stranger to the constituency did advance a considerable sum of money received from a political organisation with the in- tention of contaminating the constituency. (Cheers from the Liberal benches.) His Memory on the Subject was not very distinct, but that the person did not bear the name of Schnadhorst, nor was the organisation to be (mond in Bir- mingham, but he believed in London. (Cheers.) He re- gretted that he was unable to answer the question of the hon. member for Northampton, as he was entirely unable to contemplate such a posrtion as the bill for the further prevention of corrupt practic-s not being passed this session. ("Hear, bear," and laughter.) A Mmurrra or AGRICULTURE. Mr. GiAnsrown said that the Government had not yet been able to take any steps to carry out the resolution of the House in favour of the appointment of a Minister of Agriculture. THN hum Anaws-rs.—Mr. Fons-ran said the persons apprehended under the Coercion Act were reasonably sus- pected of being either the planners or the perpetrators of outrages, and it was possible ander the present state of things in Ireland that a man might be guilty of such a crime, and yet not be a dissolute ruffian. The regulations to which these persons were subjected were milder than those which prevailed in the case of first-class misde- meanants. , •

OnsTrencrioN.—Mr., Gladstone felicitated himself and the House on the disappearance of "obstruction," and de- clined at present to entertain the idea of making the penal- ties for that offence more stringent. CANDAHAR.—LORD lIARTINGTON stated that at present there are 4,430 British and 11,674 native troops of all arms employed in garrisoning Candabar or protecting the line of communication with that city. TRE GUNPOWDER PLOT IN TNE CITY.—Sir STAFFORD NORTE6OTE asked the Home Secretary whether he could give any information with regard to the suspicious discovery of some explAsivet materials said to have taken place at the Mansion House. (Hear, hear.)—Sir WILLIAM HatscauseT: I have receive a report on the subject, and there is no doubt that an abominable attempt was made last night to commit an outrage by an explosion of gunpowder at the Mansion House. The matter is now under investigation, and I don't think it is desirable that I should state further details at present. THE NEGOTLATIONS IN NATAL.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE: I wish to ask whether the Government can give the House any information as to what has taken place between the Boers and Sir Evelyn Wood ?—Mr. GLADSTONE : I quite agree that the question which has been put is extremely seasonable. The report in some of the newspapers than an arrangement has been come to is premature. The communi- cations with a view to such an arrangement are proceeding between Sir Evelyn Wood and the Boer leaders, but it is im- possibfe for me at the present moment to eNpree.9 any opinion as to the probable issue of such communications., 1 THE Maly ESTIMATEIL—The House afterwards welt into cemmittee.—ln moving a vote of £4,436,000, Mr: CHILDERS explained that the change which he contemplated would involve an additional charge for the present, although they would result in an ultimate ecouomy.—Colonel STAN- LEY generously recognised the useful character of the War Minister's reforms, while commenting on details. A discus- sion, sustained almost entirely by military members of the House, followed.

, - THE CHURCH PATRONAGE BILL. - Four laymen bate brought into the House of Commons a Bill dealing wi h Church patronage. It proposes to give the bishops geeatbr authority in dealing with unworthy or incompetent p - sentees ; but its most marked features are the abolition f donatives ; allowance, under conditions, of power to tie parishioners to object to the presentation of unfit person &; the legalising of exchanges for money considerations; tie abolition of the present declaration or oath against !Amon, , and the institution of another ; and the abolition of the sate of next presentations apart from advowsons. The Bill s I no doubt well meant, and as much as could be expecti, I from Mr. Stanhope and the other members who have tak n charge of it. But it is mere tinkering, not reformation, and will be utterly inefficacious in stopping the abuses of Church patronage.—Liberater.

INTS TO CORRESPONDE2VTS.—,This portion of the EXAMINER being set apart as a medium .for an interchange of knowledge between our numerous correspondents, con- tributors will greatly facilitate our labours by attending to these suggestions :--1. State in all instances the number and name of the questions to which answers are sent, 2. Write on one side of the paper only. 3. Take care that ell silmes and dates are written as plain and clear as possible. 4. Each question and each answer should be written on separate sheets of paper, and the real name or now de plume of the writer attached. 5. When it is desired that only an anonymous signature shall be published with the question or answer, then we must be supplied with the real name and address of the writer as a private guarantee to us of good faith.

div.head: SIMNEL OR MID-LENT CAKE.
div.p: THE SIMNEL OR MID-LENT CAKE.

A lady, writing on the above, says :—lt Is curious to observe how all our festivals—which, of coarse, owe their origin to the Church—are connected with some special appeal to gastronomy. The good cheer of Christmas is pro- verbial;then come the pancakes and white fish of Lent, the nice cakes and buns of Mid-Lent and Easter, and the roast geese of Michaelmas. We all eat hot-cross buns on Good Friday, but it is not every one that has a Simnel cake on her table on Mid-Lent or Mothering Sunday, as is orthodox and proper. They are really supposed to be made by dutiful daughters, who present them to their mothers as a token of filial affection at this season of the year; and, as old cus- toms seems to cling longer to regions remote from the levelling influences of cities, this and such other pious ob- servances have not yet entirely disappeared from many country districts, especially in the North of England. Man, a time have I profited by this ancient usage, and partakin., of the rich dainty cake made historical in one of Old Herrick's epigrams:—

_ I'll to thee a Simnel bring 'Clainst thou go a mothering; So that when she blesses thee, Half that blessing Moult give me. These cakes are peculiar from the fact that they are first boiled, and then baked. They are like a very rich plum cake, with plenty of candied peel and other good things enclosed in a crust of dough. In same parts of Lancashire they are as good as bridecakes. There are many reasons given for the name Simnel, the most amusing one being that a man and his wife, named respectively Simon and Nellie, quarrelled over the manufacture of a cake prepared for a feast at Easter-time just after the Lenten fast. Sim declared it should be boiled, whilst Nell contended it should be baked. High words came to blows, but matters were at last compromised and peace restored by Nell sacrificing her stool, which she had thrown in the quarrel at Sim, to make a fire to heat a saucepan to boil the cake, and Sim broke up his besom and broom as fuel for the oven in which to bake it afterwards. Thus a new and remarkable production in confectionery became known as the cake of Sim, Nel, or "Simnel," and very good it is,l can testify, notwithstanding its origin.

At Bishop Auckland, a young wspu?.n named Mary Hall, has been committed on a charge of bigamy under peculiar circumstances. It appeared she was married three years ago, when only 16 years of are, to Armstrong Hall, but as he did not supply her with either food or money she returned to her father's house. Hall's father wrote to her father about A year ago, proposing that the two should do the best for themselves, and that neither should prosecute the other. Acting on this letter, prisoner married John Simpson after telling him her position. The question of what would happen if the consumption of spirits in the workhouse were entirely disallowed was dis- cussed on Tuesday by the Preston Guardians. The medical officer solved this problem in a sentence by pointing out that what would happen would be the necessity for recourse to expensive drugs as stimulants in cases where spirits, at less cost, would answer the same purpose. As it was stated that the use of intoxicants in the workhouse was on the decrease rather than on the increase, it was resolved to make no alteration in the present arrangements. • Fir:rrry FOOD:—The Birmingham sausage case opens up a very wide and important question, and one which we have frequently discussed before. The population ef this coun- try being ahead of its powers of production, the people are driven, to a very considerable extent, to the consumption of preserved and tinned viands of various kinds. We have often pointed out the necessity of every tin or packet of pre- served provisions bearing a label setting forth the exact nature of its contents, and until this is done it can hardly be possible that persons can be convicted of cheating and adulteration, or that the many opportunities of dishonesty which now exist will not be taken full advantage of. The ' Birmingham sausage-monger was convicted of putting in his sausages material which was not fit for human consumption, owing to its putridity. This is a statutable offence, and we are glad that the offender was sent to prison without the Option of paying a fine. It is doubtful, how- ever, whether he could have been punished for put- ting horseflesh into his sausages. A "sausage " isa thing of acknowledged variability of constitution, and possibly a beef sausage might still be regarded as such, even though the beef bore but an infinitesimal proportion to the "flavour- ing." The same remarks apply to the various "potted meats," "preserved milks," "patent foods," &c. The public ought to be protected, and it is certainly proper that the percentage compositions of mannfactured. articles of con- sumption should be affixed to their containing vessels and papers. Of potted meats we need say nothing, except that respectable firms ought to be glad!? protect themselves voluntarily by a percentage composition label. We think the exact amount of sugar, or other preservative, in every tin of condensed milk, should be stated; and we think it is high tino. to take only one example, that the State should. cease to help in the gulling of the public by allowing a pennyworth of lentil-meal to be sold for 3s. ed. It isbecom- ing a question also whether manufacturers and importers of preserved and cured foods should not be placed under the Excise laws. At all events, it seems absolutely necessal7 that inspectors, similar to Excisemen, should have right of entry into the premises of manufacturers of sausages and potted meats, for it was only by a happy accident that to Birmingham fraud was discovered. Inspectors of impor foods, whether tinned or preserve& seem also a crying necea- eity, in the face of what we may call the trichinosis scare and the Welbeck

div.head: STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: THE STATE OF IRELAND.

A number of ejecttuents have been served on estates near Cashel and Balcoa, county Fermanagh, under the protection of a large body of police. A bailiff named Boyd, while serving ejectments at Moys-. town, King's County, was attacked by a tenant, and com- pelled to swear he would not serve the processes. The assailants have been remanded. Jokn O'Keane was arrested on Tuesday at Parranes under the Coercion Act. He had been absent from home since the passing of the Act. P. J. Sheridan one of the traversars in the late trial, was also arrested at Tubbercurry. A meeting of Limerick electors have called upset Mr. Gabbett to resign his seat. They offer to pay his expenses of re-election if returned again. They state that Mr. Gabber: has violated his election pledges. Each of the 20 prisoners at Kilmainham Gaol under the Protection Act has been supplied by the Ladies' Land League with bed, bedding, and some articles of clothing. One of them, Mr. Jury, has been served in prison with a process for rent, and the question will arise as to the validity of this service.

At a special sessions at Kinnelty, King's County, the charge against a man named Murphy, for the murder of John Bargen, in connection with the recent raid for arms, was to have been heard on Wednesday, but none of the wit- nesses summoned appeared. Warrants were issued for their apprehension. A report was issued on Saturday relating to migratory agricultural labourers in Ireland, and this shows that last year 42,272 agricultural labourers travelled as passengers journeying to seek employment at a distance from their homes. The major portion of these emigrants came over to England for the harvest. _ _

At County Fermanagh Assizes, Terence McAnley, charged with murdering his uncle, John Manley, by cutting his throat, pleaded guilty to manslaughter. Judge Deasy sentenced him to five years' penal servitude, saying the leniency of the sentence was owing to the fact the murder was unpremeditated, arising out of a quarrel about land. Mr. A. M. Sullivan has replied to the strictures of Arch- bishop Maccabe on the Ladies' Land League. Ili the course of his letter, he says it is terribly dangerous for any man. especially an exalted prelate of the church, to impute mo- tives or to assume to read the inner heart. He asks, as a matter of conscience, whether the archbishop is justified in thus publicly insulting and wronging some of the most ex- emplary and devoted children of the church. Mr. Nullivan says the archbishop does not like Mr. Parnell or the Land League.

At the Queen's County asaizes, John Roe, late cashier of the Maryborough branch of the Bank of Ireland, was in- dicted for having falsified his accounts, with intent to defraud, in November last. This case excited unusual interest, from the fact that it had already been tried twice at the assizes, and on each occasion the jury were unable to agree. The jury pursued the same tactics, and were dis- charged with a severe reprimand from the judge. The accused was again allowed out on bail, himself in MOP and two sureties of £5OO each, to appear at the next assizes.

Only one fresh arrest under the Protection Act was re- ported on Monday. The prisoner Boyton has informed as officer of the Land League that the American Consul who recently visited him gave him an assurance that everything that could be done for him should be done. The trial of the men charged with the murder at New Ross was on Monday postponed till the next Kilkenny Assizes, partly on account of the disturbed state of the district, and partly on account of the fact that no fewer than 171 of the persons on the jury panel were members of the Land League. In the House of Commons on Monday it was stated that no repre- sentation had been made to the Government by the Ameri- can Minister in regard to Boyton. An extraordinary occurrence has taken place at Limerick. As Captain Irwin, 20th Hussars, was passing over Matthew Bridge into the old town he felt some one pulling at his sword, and on looking round saw that it had been taken out of the scabbard, and was in the possession of a man who was running away with the weapon. Captain Irwin at once ran after the man, who, when the officer get up with him, made a lunge of the sword at the officer's breast, but fortunately without injuring him. The man then dropped the sword or let it fall, and bolted. Captain Irwin recovered the swora and at once reported the curious occurrence to the police, and on Monday morning a man named Burns was arrested on suspicion and brought before Captain Irwin, who failed to identify him. Burns was discharged. . _

The Cardinal-Archbishop of Dublin, in his Lenten to the clergy, which was read in the churches on Monday, says no doubt acts of.gross extortion, which cry to Heaven for ven- geance, have been inflicted in many cases on the half- famished tillers of the soil, and these acts cannot be digni- fied with the names of contracts. But if one of the two con- tracting parties can, without reference to any competent tribunal, modify or recind the terms of his engagement, the very foundations of society are destroyd. Referring to the Ladies' League, the Archbishop says that not at the call of charity are the women of Ireland invited to come before the world. They are asked to forget the modesty of their sex and the high dignity of their womanhood by leaders who seem utterly reckless of consequences, and who, by their recklessness, have brcught misery on many families. A sheriff's sale of horses and cattle took place on Tuesday, at Marlborough. It appears that setae of the tenants of Mr. Richara Warburton,of Garryhinen Queen's County, having refused to pay their rents unlesa they got a substantial re- duction, writs were issued against them, and their cattle and horses were seized, and were put up to auction. The animals were brought to the town under the protection of a strong escort of police and military. Mr. Goddard and three others attended on behalf of the Property Defence Association. The cattle and horses were bought in at fair prices by friends of the tenants, and after the sale the cows were paraded through the street., and their horns decorated with green ribbons. Leaves and laurel were also put round their necks, and the horses were also decorated with ribbons and laurel. Bands followed through the streets, and some of the tenants followed wearing the writs in their hats.
TRADE NOTES. It is calculated that since the collapse of the colliers' strike' in South Yorkshire the value of steam coal has diminished 2s. a ton.

_ The strike at the new Seaham Colliery is at an end. Ali • men have returned to work. Legal proceedings for breaches of contract and intimidation arc withdrawn. s. The Clyde Shipbuilders' and Engineers' Association of Employers have resolved that in future all apprentices should be legally bound for a term of years. This resolution has been aceeptea by the workmen's society. The Ashton and Oldham Coalowners' and Miners' Asso- ciation have invited, and Mr. Hugh Mason has accepted, the position of umpire in the question of advance of wages and the sliding scale.

Although three miners' associations are in existence, a movement is on foot amongst South Yorkshire miners of forming a new federation confined to miners employed at Silkstone and thin-seam collieries. Steps are said to have been taken for calling a meeting of thick-seam owners for forming a masters%associatinn. Both movements have origi- nated from the recent struggle. The quarrymen employed at Lord Penrhyn's extensive quarries at Bethesda have been informed of the owner's and manager's intention of returning to the system of four days' Working. This announeement has caused much indignation, inasmuch as the men are of opinion that the present state of the slate trade does not justify the proposed diminution in the days of working. The men employed at these works now number 3,000 odd.

div.head: ILON AND CoAL TRADES.,
div.p: THE ILON AND CoAL TRADES.,

I .ecCASHIRE.—There has been only a moderate amount of business doing in the coal trade of this district during the past week, and although the Lancashire collieries have not fully resumed their ordinary output, there is, as a rule, quite if not more than sufficient coal being raised to meet the orders coming to hand, whilst considerable quantities of Yorkshire coal are still coming into the district. The effects of the recent strike are disappearing with a rapidity which could scarcely have been anticipated ; supplies are already in excess of requirements, and any pressure in the market is now rather on the part of sellers than buyers. For house- fire coals there has been a fair demand, and for rnanufac. turing classas of fuel there has also been a tolerably good inquiry. The scarcity which was previously being experi- enced in engine fuel has, howev, for the present been removed by the increased quantity of slack thrown upon the market in consequence of the amount of coal which has been screened during the past fortnight for house-fire pur- poses, and colliery proprietors are not able to maintain the extreme prices which have been asked of late. The average quotations at the pit mouth remain at about 106 to 10s CA per ton for best coal, 75 6d to Ss 6d for second qualities, 65 6d to 7s for Common round coal for steam and forge pur- poses, 55 to 58 6d for burgy, and 3s 6d to 4s 6d for slack, according to quality. There is, however, a good deal of Pressure on the part of buyers for concessions, and prices generally are still unsettled, with a downward tendency in the market. The local coke ovens are again getting into operation, but an advance of 10d to Is 8d per ton upon late rates is generally being asked, best cokes being now quoted at 12s to Iss, and small cokes at 9s to IN per ton at the ovens. The iron trade of this district continues extremely quiet, and during the past week there has been an almost complete cessation of demand. A want of firmness is apparent throughout the market, and it is scarcely possible to say what sellers would be prepared to accept if offers were made. Lancashire makers of pig iron are now quoting, for delivery into the Manchester district, 46s 6d for No. 3 foundry and 45s 6d for No. 4 forge, less 21 per cent. These figures, however, do not lead to any orders being placed, and local makers would be open to offers. Sellers of outside brands are in many cases willing to take very low figures, but little or no business is reported. In the finished-iron trade prices are weak, and for prompt specifications makers are Willing to quote very low. The average price for bars delivered into the Manchester district is now £5 17s 6d. per ton. In the engineering and machine-making branches of trade there is still an absence of any general activity. A few of.the large firms who do a foreign trade are tolerably busy, but, as a rule, works are barely kept going, and there are very few orders on home account coming into the market.

orocedures of the Opposition, we have said that the lifficulties surrounding the Government have '4ecome less menacing than they were not c any days ago. In the first place the lochade of public business in the House of Commons ,as been broken. The Government has, indeed, bad to ask the House to adopt some new rules of pro- cedure proposed by the Speaker in order to get rid of naked obstruction, but those alterations still leave abundant scope for fair debate. A motion of urgency for any business which would stop debate is not to be considered as carried unless the majority in its favour is three to one; so that unless both the great parties consent, urgency cannot be voted. The two Irish ,bills, which had been the cause of all the contention and all the abuse of Parliamentary privileges, are passed; and even the risk of bring unable to get the votes in Supply all taken by the legal date, in conse- quence of the great waste of time in obstruction, which induced Mr. Gladstone to ask for urgency for Supply on Monday, has materially diminished. The Conservatives would not vote for urgency; but they know that the votes of Supply are wanted to pay the current expenses of the public services, and having scored a little victory, as they think, they have since been in a compliant humour, and havo allowed a 'large number of votes to pass without any discussion on their part. In this way the arrears of business are getting cleared off. By Easter, if obstruction does not again rear its ugly head, matters may after all-have been restored to their usual form. Ministers have got their disagreeable jobs done, and may presently address themselves to the more congenial tasks of shaping and advocating important reforms. Of course, Liberals fully anticipate that when remedies, not 'parities, for Irish discontent are before the House, the Opposition, as a party which does not believe in land-law amendment in the interest of tenants, will assume a posture of distinct antagonism. But the Government and Liberal majority in the House of Commons will fight the Tories on these lines with the utmost cheerfulness—with much more complacency than they have received steady Tory support whilst dealing with coercive measures. And the Liberal party throughout the country, feeling that Parliament has now got upon work which they desire and have striven to bring to pass, will experience a pleasure, an exhilaration, a heartiness strongly contrasting with the depression which the repressive proposals, how- ever indispensable, have caused in the minds of all friends of liberty and political progress. We look, too, for a favourable Budget from Mr. Gladstone, and for a courageous scheme of financial rectification and retrenchment, including, perhaps, the costs of the fag-ends of Tory wars and deficits notwithstand- ing, an instalment of a future series of reductions of taxation. These things in prospect afford pleasant sensations to the supporters of the Liberal Govern- ment, and enable us to entertain the conviction that "the winter of discontent" the nation has endured since Tory policy began to yield its bitter fruit will soon be changed to "glorious summer " by the triumphant development of that declared policy of Mr. Gladstone an his distinguished colleagues, which:comprehended the reversal of the course of Inso- lent aggressions upon inferior states; the re- establishment of the European concert on Turkish questions; the reduction of the enormous expenditure on military entetprises ; restoration of the fiscal equilibrium ; liquidation of taxes ; justice to the tillers of the land in Ireland, and in England and Scotland likewise; and large improvements of our systems of representation in Parliament and of elec- tion. Whilst the atmosphere of British policy in Parliament is being purged of stormy elements, the fogs and,vapours which have obscured it, the more distant outlook grows clearer and brighter. The con- dition of Ireland, we are assured, has altered vastly for the better with the last two or three weeks ; in India, the spontaneous withdrawment of the British forces from Candahar gives an augury of friendly understanding betwixt the Anglo-Indian Govern- ment and the Afghans; and in South Africa, ' although whilst we write the results of the negocia- tfon conducted by Sir .Evelyn Wood with the Boer leaders is not declared, we entertain a belief that a basis of peace which may be acceptable both to the people of England and of the Transvaal can be found if both parties are sincere in the desire for peace, and so the miserable alternative for the re- sumption of this nanst gratuitous of wars may be escaped, and the lives of the thousands of our soldiers who must perish in the war if it goes on may be saved for more honourable service than the exter- mination of a small settlement of Dutch Colonists, who ask only to be left to themselves in the remote territory of the African interior in which they sought i a home after being dislodged by British annexations I elsewhere.

TirE Emperor of Russia has at last fallen a victim to the relentless persistency of his enemies. The secret societies which had pledged themselves to his destruction have at length kept their word. Hitherto they had striven hard, though in vain, to accomplish their purpose, but ill-fated success has at last re- warded their:diabolical resolution. There have been Emperors who have deserved less consideration at the hands of their subjects than Alexander 11., who have, nevertheless, been more kindly treated. Although his reign was a despotic one, it has not been without its blessings to the people. If he did not accomplish for Russia all those reforms which would have placed it in front of all civilised communities, he did more perhaps by the mere exercise of his own will than any living monarch for the good of his people. He suc- ceeded an ambitious and war-loving Emperor, who strove restlessly to extend his influsnce, but the course which he adopted was very different. He proceeded at once to reduce the military expenditure, and bring the finances of the country into a healthier state. But the moSt eventful act of his reign, so far as his own subjects were concerned, was the liberation of the serfs. It cannot for one moment be contended that he was anything like a pattern to kings and princes, but when it is remembered that his policy was for a long time favourable to the development of free in- stitutions, and that be did much to elevate the people over whom he ruled, the attempts upon his life ap- pear all the more detestable. For some time past he cannot be said to have been directly responsible for the direction of Russian affairs. He might be regarded as a king without a crown, for his life, rendered insecure and miserable by the assassins, who were always on his track, was made as private as possible. But nothing has availed him. The fatal blow has at last cut him down, and the world looks on with awe. There is in this country a strong Anti- Russian party, who have reviled and abused Russia more than anything could justify. But we feel per- suaded that the indignation and horror which an atrocious deed like this cannot fail to excite, will in.- spire our countrymen without distinction of party. Englishmen have their likes and dislikes, but they do not bear the resentment of the kind that would rejoice over such a catastrophe as this. There are few men in this country who will not in their hearts, as well as with their lips, denounce in unmeasured terrus this foul and fiendish deed. With the assassin we can not have the slightest sympathy. He s ardent, 8 be is a mere beast of Prey. Let him be ever institutions tiwtuetlli on sedbuecateevde,r leto hie nthusiisa, after tsmefror ferocious brute unfit to dwell among men. We can id do admire the patriot fighting for freedom, and field in ravely risking his life in the open all, a e vindica- tion re of his claims; but the mean coward who goes about plotting in secret to take the life of OLIP who has done him no personal injury, but is merely' the representative of a system of government which he himself detests, deserves to be universally execrated and condemned.

THERE iS no doubt that the bone of contention between Churchmen and Nonconformists, in respect of the celebration and especially the registration of L.arriages, will have to occupy ths attention of Parlia- ment before long. There is a grievance„ and that grievance must be removed. There is inequality, and

div.head: EXAMINER, SITURD_AY, MARCH 19, 1881
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SITURD_AY, MARCH 19, 1881

it is to a Liberal Government that the Nonconfor- mists naturally look for redress. At present tb a Evglish State Church clergyman is constituted by law registrar in his parish, for he not only official( s at marriages but also registers them. The publi3 registrar as a representative of the Civil Govern- ment has no right to force himself upon the scene in a parish church whilst a marriage is being celebrated. But Nonconformists are dealt with in quite a different fashion. When a marriage takes place in any of .their places of worship, it is imperative that the public re- gdstar should be present, and certain words must be used and pledges taken in his hearing, otherwise the ceremony is null and void. And this is not all, the rtgistrar has to bring his register with him, and he e,etains the marriage party until he has made all the necessary entries, obtained the signatures of the con- tracting parties, the minister, and the witnesses, and collected his fees. Now, such a distinction as this is ehogether unnecessary, invidious, and galling, and is regarded by a large number of Nonconformists as an insult, so that it is high time to do away with it. A Bill has therefore been introduced by Messrs. Blenner• basset, Morley, and Errington to Parliament to alter and amend the la-a- relating to the registration of niarriages. The preamble of the bill sets out that it islawful for clergymen of the Church of England to solemnise marriage without the presence of the regis- trar, and that satisfactory provision has been made for the marriage of members of the Society of Friends and of Jews, and then claims similar privileges for the ministers of other religious bodies, sad that "thereby the marriage fees should be reduced, and lawful marriage facilitated." The bill provides that for the payment of a fee of £2 2s. 6d. the Registrar General shall register the minister as the minister of a registered place of worship, in which marriages may be solemnised without any registrar being present. It also proposes to extend the legal hours of marriage from eight to six, instead of from eight to twelve, as at present. There is also a provision that the Non- conformist minister shall register marriages at which he has officiated in books kept for that purpose, and that in the months of April, July, October, and January he shall give a copy of his register to the district registrar, retaining one for his owu use ; and the minister is to be entitled to fees for searches in his register books. I.; has frequently been stated, and not without good reason, that clergymen of the Es- tablished Church have in many instances been very slovenly and negligent in keeping marriage registers, and that it would be sound policy to compel all ministers to make way for the district registrar, but this bill includes a provision under which any such errors shall be duly corrected. The Bill further pro- vides that parties intending to be married who wish to have the registrar present, may gratify that wish by paying an extra fee varying from ss. to 10s. We have thus sketched the main provisions of the Bill, and as it would be premature to discuss its merits just now in detail we shall content ourselves with saying that it has several recommendations which Nonconformists will duly appreciate. It is intended to abolish an offensive inequality, to enable Dissenters to be married in their own places of worship without extra cost and to furnish safeguards against errors in the register. It is patent that some legislation of the kind is necessary, and we earnestly hone that our re- presentatives in Parliament will facilitate the passing of this or a similar and better measure.
