div.p: LOU iL NOTES,

The last monthly meeting of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners was of a very lively description. In the ordinary course of things, there is a scene at every fifth meeting of this body, so that by the date of the gathering mentioned, it was about time that the overcharged at- mosphere was released of some of its electricity. The old and almost threadbare question of the Infectious Diseases Hospital was upon the carpet, and the committee who have charge of the matter, have got so far as to instruct the surveyor to prepare plans of a building to contain eight beds. It may be as well, in order to prevent any misunder- standing on the part of those ratepayers who like all things done decently and in order, that I should state the commit- tee have not arrived at this decision in a hurry. They have taken their time about it, having a wholesome dread of any- thing which might have the appearance of impetuosity; as it is now about six years since the the hospital question was first mooted. It seems that owing to the difficulties of a circumlocution-office-character which have to be sur- mounted before any patient can be admitted to the present teinporary hospital, the committee recommended that no one should be received except by consent of the chairman (Mr. George Marshall). Judging from the discussions that have taken place on the hospital in the dim past, it was hardly to be expected that Dr. McDougall, who has always had some difficulty to bring forward each time the committee had reported pro- gress, would permit such a golden opportunity to pass • without giving vent to his overcharged professional feel- ings. Having indulged in a quiet sneer at the manner in which Mr. Marshall had "come to the rescue" of the medical officer, in a certain case which had been admitted, he strongly condemned the proposal to give the chairman any such power as that proposed in the minutes, and next aired a proposal which may possibly give the public the key to his opposition to the hospital scheme from its very inception. This was that an arrangement ought to be entered into by which medical men who were the regular attendants of a patient before his adMission, might be able to enter into an agreement so that they could continue their official visits after the case had been taken into the build- ing. Of course, under the supposed ordinary rules by which such an institution would be governed, if a medical man who is a Commissioner was attending a patient suffer- ing from infectious disease, be would not be able to continue to run up a bill owing to his official position preventing his so doing. Mr. Handley hit the right nail upon the head when he said that the discussion had proceeded 1 upon what apPeared to him a false assumption, viz., that Dr. Mouritz, the medical officer, was incompetent to perform his duties. The chairman said he bad no ob- jection to any member airing his professional knowledge, or 1 impugning his judgment; but he strongly censured Dr. McDougall for reflecting upon his truthfulness, in the case of a man named Whitehouse, who had been admitted to the hospital. At a later stage of the proceedings, Dr. McDougall, who is somewhat too prone to claim the chairman's indul- gence by rising to speak several times on one subject, was told by p&r. Marshall that he could not be allowed to pro- ceed unless he moved a resolution. He then said he was quite willing to propose that Mr. Marshall vacate the chair. Such an observation from a private member to the Chairman of a Board must certainly have been very irritating, and it called forth the peppery rejoinder from Mr. Marshall that he believed the Doctor had impudence enough even to do this. Dr. McDougall asked that the words might be repeated, but the chairman did not grant his request. The friends of the Doctor say that he did not hear the observation as to his impudeame, or a terrible castigation would have been administered to Mr. Marshall. It is said that a frightful storm is brewing, and that the redoubtable Doctor is deter- mined to bring forward a motion at the next meeting to the effect that Mr. Marshall vacate the chair. The next gather- ing of the Commissioners is on the 24th instant, and I should suppose that by that time it is highly probable Dr. McDougall will have forgotten all about the matter, or deter- mined to pass by what was said in the heat of debate. From a cursory glance at that embodiment of wisdom known as " Zadkiel's Almanac," I see that during March "the ap- proaching conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter now beets to disturb both the atmosphere and the political world ; " and there are to be "mutations" that will "disturb the serenity of the most peaceful peoples." Would it not be well, as such terrible things are in the air, to pursue a peaceful instead of a warlike course?

Some few weeks ago, the Runcorn Sehool Board wisely decided to take a census of the children of school age in the town; and you gave publicity to the admirable report of the clerk (Mr. Rigby) in your last issue. It would scarcely be interesting to repeat the figures given there, but I may briefly state that, after making reasonable allowances on certain grounds, there is a nett deficiency of 616 in the ac- commodation provided. During the discussion the interest- ing fact was disclosed that there are about 1,000 more children in the town than there were six years ago. This shows that Runcorn is advancing, and there is some prospect of it becoming a place of no small importance in the future. Against this I may I Owe another statement, also made by the Clerk, to the [effect that there are about 200 empty houses in the town. This is not a very pleasant state of matters for consideration by those who are owners of house property, but it must not be forgotten that of late years builders have been very busy in the town, and it may be that they have over stocked the market. Another reason for such an exceptional state of things maybe the dulness of trade.

Another attack was made upon the Highway Committee at the last meeting of the Widnes Local Board. The mem- bers of this committee appear to be in a state of obfuscation :Ls to the difference between revenue and capital account. There is but little doubt that before the departure of Mr. Darlington, the Local Government Board auditor, from the town, they will have a little 11,ht thrown upon their some - hat foggy proceedings.

The days when the usurper, man, proudly denominated himself lord of creation are at last numbered. The so-called "weaker vessel" is fast emancipating herself from the thral- dom in which she has been held during so many ages. Cavillers at the sights of women be warned in time, for the hour of your discomfiture approaches. Already has a har- binger of female equality with man made its appear sues. In the prospectus of a young lath( 8' educational establishment, which I have just received' appears the following announcement:—" Education will be conducted upon high minded principles." Is it possible that "high minded," and "strong minded " are synonymous terms in the modern lsdies' vocabulary? I fear that this is so for losveralown upon the same document I find that "Instruction is given in the political history of England." Will political instruction, I wonder, be meted out impartially to each student, or will separate classes be held for the fair partizans of Liberalism and Conservatism. Then again occurs the query as to whether each pupil will be allowed to select her own shade of political opinions, or will her parents dictate them and in the event of each fair politician being allowed to exercise her discretion what would be done if a champion of Lord Beaconsfield suddenly changed her views and became an advocate of Mr. Glad- stone's policy? Certainly after this, I would advise the young men of the present day to apply themselves to a careful study of political matters or their chances of con- nubial bliss will be greatly imperilled. What politic I 1 young lady could have any respect for an admirer, no matter how fascinating his moustache who was unable to give her the date of the Corn Law Repeal Act? 'The consequences of acting the part of the good , Samaritan sometimes prove exceedingly inconvenient and embarrassing, or at least, I think, a gentleman who played that role the other day will say so. It appears that he was returning home one evening and when near the canal lie was suddenly startled by hearing a loud splash, and on going ' towards the water he there saw a young lady battling for , her life. Without the slightest hesitation our hero sprang into the water, rescued the drowning young woman, and had her conveyed to his own residence, whhili was near at hand and where, under kind and careful treatment, she eventually recovered. This, however, was not all, for it seems that the cause of the young lady's appearance in the water was the old story—man's treachery, seduction, and base desertion. Before the young lady was in a fit state to leave the house of her rescuer a " little stranger" was added to the company, and though this submitted the resources of the establishment to an unexpected strain, both mother and child were kindly housed and provided for urn!t they could be safely removed elsewhere. Nevertheless, it must be con- fessed that it was rather an embarrassing position for a paterfamilias to be placed in. The result of an investigation by the police shows that the sensationaraccount of a man and dog fight, emanating from the Rossendale Valley, was possessed of but a modi- cum of truth. Stripped of the nauseous details supplied by a local correspondent, the affair is resolved into a miserable public-house wager by no means exciting. It was just the sort of feat that some low type of a drunkard might be ex- pected to attempt for the edification of his companions. There was no fierce fight and no blood spilt; the fictitious " Brummy "saw a bull dog sitting on a bench, and remarking to his companions that he could worry it, advanced towards it, seized it with his teeth,—as gently as he could, we may be certain, for bull dogs have it in their power to retaliate with a vengeance—lifted it off the form, and the dog then bolted out of the room. This the police assert is the true account of man and dog fight No. 2. It is more than pro- bable that future reports of man and dog fights will be ac- cepted with a grain of salt, and I would therefore advise highly imaginative scribes, who desire to go into the sen- sational to turn their energies into another direction. Whilst I have no desire to hide the shortcomings of the publicans, I can quite believe the assertion that the great majority of the members of the trade do not desire to har- bour drunken people on their premises, and I am also of opinion that in nine cases out of ten should the insatiable toper be refused the repletion of his oft quaffed cup, and his obscured senses allow him to remember the solicitude which Boniface exhibited for his welfare, lie will, on sober reflection, come to the conclusion that the publican acted the part of a friend in so doing. It is therefdre to be regretted that every thirsty individual cannot ' tske such refusal in the same philosophical spirit as was I shown by a summarily expelled customer from a neighbour- ing public-house last week. The landlord bad come to the conclusion that his customer who desired to be supplied with a "whiskey hot" had imbibed enough stimulants for one day consistent with steady and graceful locomotion, and he ' politely informed the incoherent one of his opinion on the subject. Seeing that the customer was somewhat loth to quit the counter, Boniface gave instructions to Ids barman to help the gentlemen to the out- side of the establishment—a command which was promptly and efficiently obeyed. Many foolish fellows under such cir- cermstances would have waxed wroth and created a dis- turbance which would have ended in a night's lodging pro- vided by the "gentlemen in blue." Our friend did nothing of the kind but suddenly persuaded himself that the barman was his benefactor, and thrusting his hand into his pocket for some " brass" offered them to the active individual with the apron who stood at the door watching the effect of the expulsion he had so quickly effected. The "brass " was not accepted, and the philosophical toper before commencing his zigzag journey homewards pitched them through the doorway for the barman to pick up at his leisure. FLACCUS.

div.head: NEW PAINTINGS AT ST. MICHAEL'S
div.p: NEW PAINTINGS AT ST. MICHAEL'S
CHURCII, DITTON.

The interior of St. Michael's Catholic Church, Ditton, is about to be embellished with a costly set of paintings repre- senting the Stations of the Cross. It is well known that the , Stations of the Cross are one of the favourite Catholic devo- tions. In former centuries, those which well deserve to be called the ages of faith. Christians flocked from all parts of Europe to Jerusalem, there to tread in reverent devotion the hallowed way which the Saviour of the world had gone laden with His cross from the gates of Jerusalem to the summit of Mount Calvary. Later the custom was intro- duced of setting up in churches and ather places through. out Christendom representations of the way of the cross at Jerusalem, and to stimulate the fervour of the faithful for this holy exercise of devotion, the Popes granted the same indulgences to those stations as were attached to those at Jerusalem. Hence it is that paintings or sculptures, repre- senting the Way of the Cross, are to be found in almost every Catholic church. It is an elegant set of paintings of this character that are about to grace the aisles of St. Michael's at Ditton. The church of St. Michael's is, no doubt, a beautiful building, but much remains to be done before its interior is fitted up in a manner worthy of its architectural beauty. The bare cold walls and empty aisles lack that richness and festiveness of decoration which is the pride of well-furnished Catholic churches. Something has already been done, and indeed much, for so short a time the building has been erected. A sumptuous high altar with a beautifully carved tabernacle, a large and very fine organ, a more than life-size statne of St. Antony of Padua, and several beautiful stained glass windows, are what have been brought to stand within a year or two of the opening of the church; and the energy and generosity, that has done so much in so short a time, is a guarantee that much more will be done in the near future. But what will contribute more than anything else has hitherto done to beautify St Michael's are the fourteen large and beautiful Statigns of the Cross to which we have referred. 'These pictures, which the writer has already had the pleasure of seeing and inspecting, are oil-paintings in canvas tastefully set in oak frames carved in the Romanesque style. Each painting, taken with its frame, measures 9 feet, with the cross 10 feet by 4 feet 8 inches. They are to some extent copies of the celebrated work of the well-known artist, the late Carl Fahrich, of Vienna, who has justly earned a high reputation as a Christian artist of pure and holy inspiration. The paintings have been executed in the Kunstverlag or firm of Frederick Gypen, at Munich, the German capital of Christian art, and are undoubtedly worthy of the firm and the art-renowned city from which they come. Each station presents to us a group of five or six figures representing the prominent characters in each stage of the mysterious drama that unfolds itself before our eyes. There are no unnecessary figures crowded on the canvas, while the back ground of the picture is plain, being nothing more than a portion of the walls of Jerusalem, or the hills behind. The effect of this arrangement is that the eye, undistracted by anything of a secondary or merely accessory character, reposes tranquilly on the central figure of the Saviour and the group of persons actually engaged around Him. The features and attitude of the several characters are rendered with great expression, vividness, and accuracy of detail, so that the impression given by each station is that of a tableau vivant presented to the eye. If we may venture to compare where all is so good, we shall be inclined to think that the Twelfth Station, representing the Death of our Saviour on the Cross, is that on which most pains have been bestowed, and which is hence pro- bably the finest in execution, as it is the most striking in expression. But more we need not say. We have been given to understand that the paintings will he solemnly set up in the church on Sunday, the 27th inst. There will be High Mass and sermon in the morning, and in the afternoon the ceremony of blessing the stations and opening them to the devotions of the faithful. A visit to the church on that day will be an occasion of witnessing an interesting ceremony, and of seeing the new paintings under the most favourable circumstances.—Com.

ALBEET-EOAD BAND OF HOPE, WintiEs.—A public meeting and entertainment was held in connection with this society, in the chapel, on Monday evening, and was very fairly attended notwithstanding the very wet weather.

CHILD DROWNED AT RUNCORN. —On Thursday. an inquest was held at the Boathouse Inn, Runcorn, on the body of Em ma Mac Kay, aged eight years, who was found in the Old Quay Deck on Wedrijsday afternoon. The deceased was the daughter of a woman who, in the early part of February, was staying at Higgins's lodging-house, Mersey-street, and said she came from Wales, and was in search ef her husband, who had deserted her. On the 13th ult. deceased went out to play, and was reported missing the .4aine evening. Information was given to Superintendent Williamson, who inserted a description of her in the Police Ga:ette. The jury returned an open verdict.
BENCORN.—NELSON STREET BAND or HOPE.-Mr. C. Garnett presided at the meeting of this society on Monday evening, and at the close 16 people signed the pledge.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS' ELECTION. - The nominations close on the 26th inst.
WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—It is rumoured that Mr. Thomas Handley, ironmonger, will be one of the candi- dates at the coming election. .
Runonx ST. JOHN'S BAND OF HOPE. At the meeting., on Wednesday night, Mr. James Kirkham presided, and addresses were delivered by Mr. John Humphreys and Mr. Booth.
IVIDNES POSTAL MATTERS.—A letter box has been placed in the wall of the arch adjoining the London and North- Western Station, and it will be emptied at 9.50 a.m. and 7.56 p.m,

DITTON AND THE FOOT-AND-MOUTH DisEAsE.—The re- turns as to the foot-and-mouth disease, show that it has broken out on the premises of Mr. Joseph Longton, of Ditchfield Hall, Ditton, six cows being affected out of a herd of twelve.

THE REIMITITE METGODISTS AT ROCK SAVAGE.—A ser- vice of song, entitled " The Great Teacher," was given, in , connection with the Primitive Methodist Mission, at Rock ; Savage, on the 11th inst. Mr. James Stubbs, of Runcorn, conducted; and Miss Morton acted as accompanist. Si. AMBROSE CHURCH, HALTON VIEW, WIDNES.—It is announced that this new church will be opened for divine service on the 2Sth inst., when, at the afternoon service, the Right Rev. the Lord Bishop of Liverpool will Preach. The evening service will commence at half-nest seven, and the seraton will be preached IT the Venerable Archdeacon Bardsley. HOLY TRINITY YOUNG MEN'S CIIHISTIAN ASSOCIA- TION.—At the usual weekly meeting, on Monday last, the evening was devoted to impromptu speaking, and some very good speeches were delivered by most of those present on some very interesting topics, such as Nihilism; Transvaal annexation; the volunteer movement; British prestige; Paruellites; self-denial; capital punishment ; the assas- sination of the Czar; and others.

RUNCORN ANp THE CENSUS. - The twelve enumerators appointed for Runcorn and the eight outlying townships in the Runcorn registrar's district will commence the delivery of the schedules on the 28th inst. These will require to be filled up by householders on the evening of the 3rd April, and they will be collected on the following day. The work of taking the census as to ships and boats will be undertaken by the Custom House Officials. FavroN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SCIOETY.—OR Mon- day evening, Mr. J. Gamon read a paper on "Men of Mark." The Rev. J. Bateman presided. The essayist briefly referred to the following great men :—G. Washington, Howard, Romilly, Wilberforce, R. Raikes, D. Livingstone, T. Carlyle, and Lord Beaconsfield. He gave a Biwa sketch of the latter Premier's life, giving him more attention than the others. A discussion ensued, in which the following gentle- men took part :—Messrs. T. Miller, S. Barrow, A. E. Davies, and R. Hughes. There was a good attendance of members.

A COMMERCIIL TRAVELLER'S HORSE DROWNED AT WESTON POINT.—On Tuesday evening, Mr. Phipps, traveller to Messrs. Smith, of Chester, went to Weston Point in his horse and trap for the purpose of seeing some customers. When opposite Captain Clarke's house he proceeded to tie his horse to the rails, but it became unruly and refused to submit. Mr. Phipps made 1. desperate attempt to turn the horse round, but it proved unsuccessful, backed into the dock, and was drowned before it could be rescped. The horse was only bought a week previously, and was n valu- able one.

Sr. PATRICK'S DAY AT WIDNES.—This day passed off very quietly in Widnes. The sveather was of a beautiful description, and a large number of pedestrians were abroad. In the evening St. Patrick's Amateurs gave an entertain- ment in the Volunteer Hall, the first part cf which appro- priately consisted of the patriotic drama of " Rakers Emmett," Mr. S. Quinn took the title role; Miss Re y, Maria, Emmett's wife; and Miss Farrell, Judy O'Dougherty. The other members who assisted were Messrs. T. Stoner, T. Mulvaney, J. Gordon, J. Bird, M. Broffy, J. Quinn, J. Car- rel, M. Whelan, and M. Campbell. Mr. S. Gaudy's string band was in attendance, and at the close the audience sang "God save Ireland."

CREWE BRITANNIA V. RTINCORN.—The above clubs met at Crewe on Saturday last, when a very exciting game en- sued, which ended in a victory for the home team, by a goal, a disputed try, and 3 minor points, to a touchdown. Packed scrimmages were the rule during the first part, and at half time only a point had been registered. The second half was very fast and loose, the ball often finding its way from one goal line to the other, and when near the visitors' goal Bailey succeeded in scoring a try for the Britons, which Appleton neatly converted into a goal. Oilier also made a clever run and touchdown behind the Runcorn goal line, when an objection was raishl, hut the home team suede an attempt at a goal, which, however, failed. For the visitors H. Hughes, Sherlock, Andrews, Wright, and Broady showed well to the front; whilst Bailey, Oilier, Greensmith, and Harcistaffe did good service for the Britannia. After the game a tea was provided at the Imperial Hotel, and a pleasant evening was spent. CONCERT AT WIDNES.—Tho twelfth of the series of entertainments in connection with the Widues Parish Church Sunday schools was held in the Waterloo-road Achoolroom, on Monday evening. The concert consisted of vocal and instrumental music. The instrumentalists were Messrs. White, Steed, and Thorpe, violins; Mr. Simkins, violoncello; and Mr. Reclyard, contra-bass: and they were very well received. Messrs. Thorpe, 'White, Simkins, aim ' Redyard gave" Angels ever bright and fair," and Mr. Thorpe and Mr. Imison the" Austrian Hymn," a selection for violin land piano. Both pieces went very well. The song, "He wipes the tear front eviry eye," was carefully rendered by Miss Broads, and was well received, as was the air, "If with all your hearts ye truly seek Me," by Mr. White. Mrs. J. Wright-Williams was very successful in her song, "Low at Thy feet," for which she received a hearty encore, a similar I compliment being paid Mrs. White for her rendition of the air, "I know that my Redeemer liveth." The glee class I sang "How beautiful upon the mountains," "Oh taste and I see," and "Lord of all power and might," which were warmly applauded. The programme terminated with the chorale, "Holiest, breathe an evening blessing." INQUEST ON A WAGONER AT: RUNCORN.—OR Tuesday an inquest was held before Mr. T. J. Ridgway, county coroner, at the Barleymow Inn, Church-street, Runcorn, on the body of John Ellis, aged 16, of No. 35, Back Cooper-street, a wagoner, who was found dead on the line of rails running along the Weston end of the docks, and belonging to the Bridgewater Navigation Company, on the 14th inst. The evidence showed that deceased was found by John Davis, a dock labourer, at about twenty minutes to twelve, noon, whilst on a journey to the Alfred dock. Deceased was lying under the wagon which he had been driving. His left foot was very bruised, the back of his head was cut, and his brains protruding. Drs. Robinson and Bagnall were sent for, and examined the body, after which deceased was re- moved to his own home under the direction of Sergeant McMichael. A girl was called, who said she saw the horse attached to the deceased's wagon fall, as if it had been knocked down through the chain which fastened it catching something between the rails ; but she could not give a clear account of how the accident to the animal caused the injury to deceased. The jury returned a Yerdict of " Accidental death."

Flour sold moderately at generally 2d per mutat advance. Mixed American Indian corn met with a fair trade, at id more money; white was also dearer, but round sold at lower figures; the quotations were— mixed old, Is qd to 5s 7d; new, Is sid white. Is 8d ; and round, 5s Rd to its 8d per cental. Beans firm, and fairly taken at 7s 4d to is Id per lOOlbs for Egyptian Saidi. Peas quiet at late Currencies; Canadian at 6s 10d to 6s lid per eental. Oats steady but slow. Oatmeal scarce, at full prices. Here, however, many spinners and manufacturers ale well sold, and in such cases fit mness is the yule or even a nominal advance._

Futures opened strong, in respon.e to the advance of about 30 points at .t; ew York, and prices gained I-16d to 3-32 d, but there are now free sellers at the advance, and in some instances a slight reaction has taken place. Shoulders inactive. Lard: The weather and prices favour buyers. Cheese firmer. Little doing in Butter.

So far there is no increase of demand, and purchasers of goods are only disposed to buy at very low prices indeed. Yarns are a shade firmer though not distinctly better to sell. .

Messrs. Arthur Bennett, John Hankey, and Jos. WARRINGTON OPERATIVE BAKERS AND CONFECTIONERS. —The tenth annual dinner of the Amalgamated Union of Operative Bakers and Confectioners was held at Mr. Potter's, the White Hart, Market-place, on Saturday last, whenabont forty guests and members sat down to dinner. Invitations had been sent to several of the master bakers, of when.' Messrs. 'Davies, . Strange, Caldwell, Lazenby, Moore, and Cross (of. Penketh), were present. The secretary read letters from Messrs. Fairclough, Litton, Pierpoint, and Carter expressing regret at not being able to attend. After the cloth was removed Mr. Samuel Davies was unanimously elected to the,chair,, and returned thanks on behalf of the masters for the kind invitation, and said he hoped they should meet again on a similar occasion to express that good feeling thatehould exisr.between employers and employed. After a few remarks from Messrs. Moore and Caldwell, the remainder of the evening was spent in an enjoyable manner.

THE INDIAN ZOEDONE COMPANY (LIMITED). This com- pany with a capital of £lOO,OOO in shares of .£1 each, has been established to buy irons the ' Zoedone Company, Limited, the patent for the manufacture of Zoedone in India (including Ceylon, and Eurmah), together with the re- gistered trade mark and the exclusive right to manufacture, and sell Zoeddne in those places in consideration of £25,000 in cash, and twenty founders' certificates, which entitle the holders to a distri- bution of one-half the surplus profits in any year in which the shareholders shall have received a dividend of 20 per cent. The founders' certificates will be issued to and held by the Zoedone Company, Limited. Zoedone is particularly suited as a beverage for hot and enervating climates; and great as has been its success in this country, a still greater demand for it is confidently anticipated in Idnia, where a restoring and stimulating, but non-alcoholic, liquor, is almost a necessity of daily life. Numerous applications for the privilege of establishing agencies in various parts of the India have been received by the Zoedone Company. Medical • testimony of the most abundant character has fully corrobo- rated the especial suitability of Zoedone for tropical climates, and particularly for India. Zoedone being absolutely non-alcoholic, but at the same time essentially stimulating and invigorating, will, it is believed, soon become in great demand amongst the many classes in India who are for- bidden by their caste and religion to drink alcohol In any form. It is intended to erect in differeot localities manu- factories for natives as well as Europeans, with the view of enabling the former to satisfy themselves by personal inspec- tion that in all the processes of the manufacture of Zoedone their religious and caste prejudices will be rigidly respected. Zoedone can be manufactured in India at the cost of about the same as in England, and so give an ample profit if sold even at the present English price. The Zoedone Company in England ii an exceedingly profitable one; and in inviting subscriptions for shares, the directors do so in the confident belie that the enterprise is of an exceptionally sound and profitable nature. Fuller particulars will be found in our advertising columns.

div.head: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN.
ST. PETER'S Cnurten, NEWTON.—The second Lenten sermon by selected preachers was preached in this church, on Sunday last, by the Rev. James , Carson, curate of Winwick. .

BAPTIST CHAPEL, EARLESIOWN.—Tb9 ground for the new chapel in connection with this body was measured out a week ago, and a Qumber of men are now engaged cutting out the foundation. It is conveniently situated near Market- street, a few hundred yards from the Earlestown Parish ' Church. The estimated cost is about £1,200, and will he finished about September. EARLESTOWN LIBERAL Crum—The committee of this club are wisely and advantageously arranging for a bowling green for the recreation of its members during the summer months. The green is situated in Houghton-street, Earles- town, and will be kept entirely for the use of the members, without any additional charge being added to the present yearly subscription. WESLEYAN CHAPEL, EARLESTOWN. The series of Evabgelical services, conducl•ed by Messrs. Dawson and Woolley, of Weardale, and Leeds, were brought to a close on Sunday evening, when a large congregation was present. The services have been both instructive and gratifying in all respects.

LIBERAL CLIIB.—An interesting and able piper was read on Thursday cvening at the Earlesto vn Liberal Club by Mr. Henry Dagnall, entitled " Abstiacts from the teachings and doings of the past Session," by Handel Cossham ; I.llr. Lauf:van in the chair. Messrs. Gleeson, Hollyhawk, Howard, and Jenner took part in the discussion, which was very animated, it turning fhefiy upon Iriah affairs. FATAL ACCIDENT AT THE HANANNAH PIT, NEWTON-LE- WILLOWS.—EarIy_ on Saturday morning, Thomas Potter, fireman, and Joseph Woodward, labourer, descended the above pit, and proceeded to clear away some rubbish from a portion of the workings. They had not been long at work When a heavy fall of largo stones and a quantity of earth took place, which fell upon them and buried them. Imme- diately steps were taken to extricate the men. When got at, rottcr was found to be quite dead, and Woodward died immediately after being brought to the eye of the pit. Potter Was a married man, residing at Parr, and Woodward was single, living at St. Helens. The inquest was held on Tuesday, before Mr. Dritheld, when, after a careful inquiry, a verdict of "Accidental death " was returned. Orsumn AT THE MARKET HOTEL, EARLESTOWN. On Tuesday evening a grand dinner was given at Mr. W. Mell- ing's, on the occasion of the completion of extensive additions to his establishment ; about 80 friends and members of the C. M. Club sat down. The chair was taken by Mr. Brass- ington. On the removal of the cloth, the chairman ?roposed several complimentary toasts, which were heartily responded to. During the evening songs were sung by Messrs. Clark, Naylor, Read, Swan, Boud, and Williams. Mr. Cooke accompanied with good taste. CONSERVATIVE CLIITH FOR THE NEWTON POLLING DIS- Teict—A meeting of the committee of the above, with a few friends, was held at Earlestown, on Thursday evening. The principal business was to ratify the action of the com- mittee in purchasing the premises of Mr. Sanderson, butcher, Earle-street, Earlestown, with a view of converting the pre- mises into the proposed Conservative Club. The site is central, and suitable for the purposes of a club.

div.head: WARRINGTON LITIRARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON LITIRARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.

A meeting of this society was held in the Lecture-room of the Museum, on Thursday evening, Mr. J. Dun, the president. in the chair. There was a large attendance of members. Mr. Charles Gatty, of Liverpool, read a paper on "Ideals of Christian art," illustrating his subject with photographs exhibited on a screen by mean of the lime light His delineations of the subjects the photographs were intended to represent were very complete and interesting. Mr. GATTY said he wished to lay down this main prin- ciple that all works of art, whether brick-bats, tables, furni- ture, or pictures, were the outcome of two faculties in man. The first was the faculty of usefulness, which led him to obtain from the material creation everythinr, he wanted, and the other was the faculty which delighted in the divine' beauty of the works of God. These did not hold un- disputed sway, but were counteracted and stultified by our excesses, vanity, ignorance, insincerity, and greedi- nees. The lecturer exhibited photographs showing how different artists treated various subjects, In some, qualifies of a low, debasing kind were pourtrayed, whilst in others the noble and intellectual facnities were given prominence. In concluding his lecture, Mr. Getty said there was much talk in the country about educating poor people by means of pictures and sculpture, but they would be totally unfitted for such a dignified, great work unless they pourtrayed the noblest and most exalted ideas of human life. The examples he had brought before them that evening had been simply to show the various lower and higher ideals in art, and that, without laying stress upon any particular set of ideas, they might see that certain of them contained a depth of religious feeling, which came from the highest Points in the character of those persons who had produced them, and that they appealed to the highest principles of those for whom they were intended. It behoved those who were interested in the subject of bringing art more into the education of this country to see that what was done was really and entirely shscere and great and noble, or else it would fall into the hands of cheap artists, and the whole thing would be done without regard to the style of the pictures, and would degrade the artists' profession and the whole community. Mr.' T. G. RYLatqns proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Gatty for his interesting and instructive paper. lie did not think he had been more pleased with any paper read before the Society than that they had heard that night, and it was so suggestive that he did riot know where to begin to say anything about it. It had shown them that there was truth and untruth in art, and that it was the real represen- tation of the otherwise hidden life of people. He recommended them to give their mind to the subject as one that woulddo much not only to bring about a better style of art, but a state of mind in themselves which would be of benefit. Mr. Monnis seconded the motion. Mr. RATREONE, of Liverpool, in resporm to a call from the chairman, supported the proposition. The ideals of death spoken of by Mr. Gatty had shown that there was a sincere and an insincere art, and that it did not platter what the subject was so long as it was sincerely and honestly carried out. Ile then spoke of the different manner in which death had been represented in different ages, and remarked that he could have liked Mr. Gatty to have en- larged more on that subject. (Bear, hear.) Mr. GAM, in reply, said institutions of that kind (museums) must be of necessity intended for the poor, and it seamed to him that teaching of the kind they had had that night Should be given for their benefit. In order that 4 the institution should become an educator of poor men who could not read books, they ought to give them an oppor- tunity of learning from the best sources the finest teaching in the world. The meeting than terminated.

A NEW PORT OF ARRIVAL FOR COTTON SHIPS. An important movement is on foot amongst the Oldham limited companies to change the port for receiving cotton (as far as Oldham is concerned) from Liverpool to Garston. To give effect to this, about thirty representatives went to Garston to receive a vessel which had arrived with 1,700 bales of cotton from New Orleans. The vessel, the Porto, duly arrived, and the cotton is to be delivered to a number of limited companies in Oldham. The Oldham Cotton Spinning Company have sesolved in future to ship all cotton at Garston, instead of at Liverpool. Two American ships have already arrived at the latter place with cotton.

PERPETUAL PENSIONS. At the annual meeting of the Burnley Liberal Executive, a resolution was passed with acclamation in favour of the abolition of perpetual pensions and calling upon all Liberal members to support Mr. Braddugh's motion on that subject. It was stated that Mr. Rylands, the borough member, had promised to support the motion of inquiry into these pensions. A resolution of confidence in the Government was passed and ordered to be transmitted to Mr. Gladstone.

REPORTED SETTLEMENT OF THE QUESTION. CONSTANTINOPLE, Thursday Evening.—lt is stated that the Ambassadors have agreed to accept the line of frontier offered in the Turkish Note of October 3rd, in addition to the Island of Crete. Mr. Goschen alone is said to have in- sisted upon a,line comprising Tricala, Metzovo, and Larissa, but the British Ambassador is said to have finally given way. The sitting of the Ambassadors, which was to have been held to-day, has been postponed until Saturday. It is believed that the Ambassadors will send to their respective Governments the proposals agreed upon by them.

THE CABINET. Summonses were issued yesterday afternoon for Cabinet Council to be held at two o'clock to-day at the Premier's official residence.

THE NATIONAL LIFEBOAT INSTITUTION. It was stated at the annual meeting of the National Life- boat Institution that during the past year the lifeboats of the Institution have been the means of saving 577 lives from wrecked or endangered vessels. During the same period fire of the lifeboats capsized, with a loss of 18 of their crews, a number unpreoedented within one year in the history of the Institution. In the month of January last, during the violent storms, 150 lives were saved in addition to six vessels. The number of lives saved during the 57 years from the establishment of the Institution is 27,603, and in that time the sum of £538,000 has been expended on lifeboat stations and other means for saving life from ship- wreck. The society has voted 95 gold medals, 931 silver medals, and £64,000 in pecuniary rewards for saving life. The Institution has now ,270 lifeboats under its immediate control. THE TRANSVAAL. The meeting of the Transvaal Independence Committee was held at Westminster Palace Hotel, yesteaday, at which a resolution was adopted expressing satisfaction with the intention of Her Majesty's Government in entering into negotiation with the people of the Transvaal, soda hope that their independence will be secured.

div.p: HEAVY GALE AND WRECK OP A STEAMER.
A heavy gale was raging on the Clyde yesterday. The screw steamer Pioneer was wrecked off Dumbarton Castle, the crew being, however, saved. Dumbarton Pier is also damaged.

THE TRANSVAAL.—Sir S. NORTIICOTE asked if the Gov- ernment had any fresh information to communicatg as regarded the negotiations with the Boers, and whether the Transvaal vote would be taken on Monday ?—Mr. GLAD- STONE said they were not then in possersion of any fresh information. He could not say whether they would be in receipt of conclusive information before Monday: The Transvaal vote was of a retrospective character, and incon- venience would arise if it was postponed. AFOHANISTAN.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked if it was true that any offer bad been made by the Ameer Abdur Rahman. Lord Hanalsmvosrsaid the statement in the Times wa,s in- accurate as regarded affairs at Afghanistan. He hoped to be enabled to make a statement on the subject on Mon- day. ;.nrE GREEK FIIONTIRR QUESTION --Sir C. DILER Said no settlement of the Greek frontier question bad yet been arrived at.

EASTER HOLIDAYS.—Mr. GLADSTONE Could not then say on what date the House would rise for Easter holidays. THE ASSASSINATION OF THE EMPEROR OF RIISSIA.—Lord KENSINGTON, LIS Lord Controller of Her Majesty's house- hold, brought up Her Majesty's answer thanking the House for its address of condolence on the death of her ally and relative the late Emperor of Russia.—Mr. GLADSTONE an- nounced that a communication bad been received from the Russian Ambassador expressing the present Emperor's warmest thanks to both Houses of Parliament for their sympathy on tke melancholy occasion. SUPPLY: THE NAVY ESTIMATES.—The House went into committee of supply on the navy estimates. Mr. TREVELYAN explained the several changes it was proposed to introduce, and in the course of his return to the system of limited competition for first appointments in place of that of nomination, he mentioned the great improvements in- tended to be made in the medical service of the navy, and also in the Royal Marines. The number of men asked for was 358,100, including 13,000 royal marines. Ile deferred his observations on spirit rations to men until next vote was under consideration. He explained the work proposed to be done during the year. The Ajax and Agamemnon were to be finished, and the Conqueror pushed forward, and Colossus, Polyphemus, Majestic, forwarded, and Pembroke and Col- lingwood began. It was proposed to lay down two new ironclads of great speed and power, one at Portsmoath, the other At Chatham, and a considerable number of new torpedo boats of great speed and power were also to be con- structed. With regard to the present conditions of the fleet, they had now 41 ironclads with boilers in good condi- tion. Touching on the subject of armament, he said they would have a supply of heavy breechloaders by next year. —Mr. SMITE generally approved of the programme sub- mitted, and had no objection to raise against the vote asked.-Sir E. REED adversly criticised the proposals of the Board of Admiralty as regarded the construction of ironclads. He regretted large vessels were to be constructed instead of useful small ones.— Sir .J. HIS insisted on the necessity of immediate attention being given to the claims of engineer officers. To be in a satisfactory condition we ought to have over sixty ironclads in good fighting condition, whereas the Secretary of the Admiralty had stated we had only 41.—Mr. MACLITER also urged that engineer officers should be placed in such a position as to give them full command over the magnificent machinery which they had placed under their control.—Mr. BROADIMRST regretted all mention of the claims of engineer officers had been ommitted in the statement of the Secretary to the Admiralty.—After observations from Mr. Bruce and Captain Price,

THE COWLEY MIDDLE SCHOOLS, ST. HELM. Sir,—A few weeks ago a meeting was held at the Town Hall to take into consideration the best way of raising the remainder et the money required to complete the above schools, which I am sorry to say are now standing at the top of Cowley Hill in an unfinished state. At that meeting a committee of gentlemen was appointed to canvass subscrip- tions, but from what I hear those subscriptions are very difficult to get hold of. Now Mr. J. B. Leach, ever ready with a good suggestion, told the meeting that the money could soon be raised by having a sort of industrial exhibi- tion on a varied if not on an extensive scale; but this was not received in a very appreciative spirit, some sanga me individual remarking that an exhibition was all very well to raise some thL usands of pounds, but a paltry two thousand, pshaw ! As the required sum is not forthcoming, would it not be a wise thing to go in for the several thousands which can be obtained by the scheme suggested by Mr. Leach, so that the governors of the school may have a surplus to begin with.—Yours, 43c., March 17th, 1881. SARAH COWLEY'S GIiOST.

CANDOUR OR CANDAHAR. Sir,—We English are just now engaged in dis Cussing the question of making reparation, in two instances, for injuries inflicted upon other nations. Having stolen some property and murdered many of its owners, we are now hesitating whether to give back to its rightful owners that which we so wrongfully wrested from them. The lives we have wasted can never be restored; but should there be one moment's hesitation in evacuating Candahar, and restoring to the Boers their country and constitution? That there should be in free and " Christian" England men found capable of opposing so obvious an act of national reparation, is apt to lower one's opinion of the much vaunted English justice and love of fair dealing. No considerations of policy or prestige should come between us and the too-long delayed acts of righteous restoration and restitution of Candahar and the Transvaal. They are not ours, and we have no right with them. Our friends, the Tories, who are responsible for these deplorable defections from national integrity, may tell us there is a wide difference between policy and probity. They appear to be afflicted by a kind of moral blindness when viewing things politically. According to their creed, that which in the individual is rank felony is, when seen in the multitude, called a nation, a mere peccadillo. Strange influence of arithmetic upon morality! The Tories are fond of calling themselves Conservatives, which I take to mean the desire to preserve that which they have already get; that is, their own. Now, it seems they wish to extend this conservancy to the possessions of other people. The staunch upholders of constitutional rights at home ought to be more chary of trampling upon those of other people abroad.—l am, Ize. JOHN PEERS.

LOCAL EXAMINATIONS IN MUSIC. Sir,—The authorities of Trinity College' London, have just decided to revise their regulations, with s. view to still further extending the musical operations of the college. I should be glad to call the attention of your numerous readers to the advantages now offered by its local examina- tions in elementary musical knowledge, which are by far the most extensive and important of any held in this country. The national prizes, which will be awarded this year, as usual, by Sir Julius Benedict, are t 3 be four in number— viz., a first prize of £5 and a second prize of £3 in each of the two divisions, senior and junior. These prizes will be open to all, including the candidate from this centre; and, in addition, local prizes will be awarded, on the results of these examinations, to the best candidate in our own centre. I shall be glad if those interested in the spread of sound musical education will encourage and foster local talent and industry by subscribing to the local prize fund (which has already been established) sums ranging from ss. to £lls. Prizes have been given in many other local centres through- out the country with excellent results, and the Academical Board, in London, have kindly undertaken to adjudicate all such local prizes, without any further fee upon the work of the next annual examination in June. I will not encroach upon your space by giving any further particulars here; but it any of your readers should wish for further information, I shall be very pleased to give it. I will oily add that, although the unprecedented num- ber of over five thottsand candidates entered for the various local examinations in music—both practical and theoretical —held by the college last year, there are indications of a 'still larger number presenting themselves in the present year. This clearly shows the wonderful progress which is being effected in the study of music throughout the United Kingdom, and I trust that we, in this district, may be able to prove by a goodly muster at the forthcoming examina- tions that we are by no means behind the times. The examinations in Jane next comprise elementary theory, singing, and pianoforte playing, the organ, or har- monium—Your obedient servant, G. NEWCOMBE,
Honorary Local Secretary for the Warrington, Widnes, and Runcorn Centre. _ _ .

THE LAND QUESTION. have read the vapeur of your correspondent "H. W.," and have endeavoured to extract from it some little common sense and logical reasoning, but have failed to do so. If I had time and inclination, I could go through his disconnected sentences and coatrovert them in detail. I will satisfy myself by merely referring to one or two. Although "H. W." travels into various subjects utterly remote from the land question, the burden of his soul is evidently that the land of this country belongs to the people, and that the present owners are robbers. From that, therefore, it may be pretty safely concluded that "H. W." has no land. Now, I do happen to possess a few acres of land, which I have pur- chased and paid for out 9f My Es-rings, and I heye purchased that land as an investment for MOlll Which I have worked for and saved during some yeafs o/ my life. Now, having , Erst worked for and earned and saved the money, and then having Invested it in that land, I should like to know how it is that "H. W." makes out that my land belongs to the people, and that I am a robber. Now, what applies to me and my few acres also applies to the great bulk of landowners and land in this country. Land is continually being bought and sold, and those who have the money can purchase. Land simply represents money, or capital, like any other hind of property. lam quite willing to admit that some family estates have descended for generations from one to another, but what of that ? Such estates form the ' capital or money investments of those families, and if they chose to keep their money or capital invested in land, why should not they do so? W." may just as well contend that the funds of this country (consols and all the rest) belong to the people and not to the persons who have in- vested their mot.ey therein. The simple fact is that society is formed of two great classes—those who have property and those who have none-- and to the latter probably "H. W." belongs. The first class comprises people who have inherited and retalued and not squandered their patrimonies, and those who not having been born to wealth have by their own industry and talents ac- quired wealth. The second class comprises that hetero- geneous multitude made up of people whenever had, and never will have anything, and people who, having had, have run through what they had. No man belonging to the former class would for a mcment advocate the distribution of his property amongst the people. I can readily under- stand however that W.' having no land would appre- ciate such a distribution. There are various other points in "H. W.'s " production which I could attack, but it is really not worth while spend- ing time over them. One, however, catches my eye, which I will notice. He says "the land tax, which in ISOO was about £2,032,000 per annum, is now reduced by redemption to about one-half that amount." Now;what does "H. W." mean? Does he mean to insinuate that the landowners who have paid a capital sum to Government for the redemp- tion of their land tax are robbers because they do not go on paying the annual tax which they redeemed? If they have paid about 35 years' purchase for the redemption, which purchase money is by the future interest thereof to repre- sent the tax which they havb redeemed, what iniquity is there in the fact that they have ceased to pay the tax? I would recommend "H. W." to study the subject a little more, and to rest assured that we have not yet in England descended to the depths of Communism. Let him learn and then advocate the stern manly qualities of work- ing for and saving money and purchasing land, and then I have no doubt he will be able to acquire ;some without rob- bing those whe have already become the possessors by such meana.—l am, air, your obedient servant, J.

WIGAN ELEcrrox Prrirto The petitioners against the return of Mr. F. S. Powell as member for Wigan will be represented by Mr. Day, Q.C., and Mr. Biron—the counsel previously named not being able to attend in consequence of their parliamentary practice. The inquiry will open next Wednesday in the Wigan Borough Courts, and, in consequence of the limited space, the Mayor has given notice that admission will be chiefly by ticket. ' A larg number of witnesses have already been subpoenaed.
ANOTHER STRIKE AT ST. HELENS.

We stated in our last iesue that the miners in the employ of Messrs. Pilkington Brothers resolved, on Thursday night, to stop work if they were not paid on Friday nights and that they decided to work no more than five days a ! week and have Saturday as a holiday. According to the statement of Mr. Cross, miners' agent, the manager of the works bad promised them weekly pays, the pay days to be on Fridays; but this he has refused, and the men struck work on Friday night. On Monday, at noon, a meeting of the men was held on the Fair Ground, about 200 miners be- ing present. Mr. John Pranter presided, and the meeting was addressed by Mr. Cross, who said that this was not another strike, as they were simply asking that the agree- ment which had been entered into be carried out. He pro- tested against the way in which Mr. France conducted him- self when approached by a deputation; and if they took his (the speaker's) advice they would not go near any of the pits which were superintended by Mr. France.—Mr. John Tranter addressed the men, and said he was sorry to read that a rev, gentleman in thenown had been rebuking the colliers for preferring begging to work. He for one would much rather work than beg, and if there were no other course open to him he would do that very unwillingly. He proposed the following resolution, "That we go to work to- morrow (Tuesday), but that we only work five days of nine hours each day, a week, whatever the consequences might be."—The resolution was carried unanimously. On Tuesday morning the men went to their work, but will leans off work on Friday night, when they hope to be paid their wages. A tabulated statement has been published "of miners' wages at St. Helens Colliery Company, belong- ing to Messrs. Pilkington Brothers, for the fortnight ending the 10th of the present month, since the late strike." This list shows that the gross wages average 3.s 7d per day. "All stoppages are to come off this, leaving 3s per day for each man nett."

div.head: ST. HELENS BICYCLE CLUB.
div.p: ST. HELENS BICYCLE CLUB.

The members of this club, which is one of the largest in England, had their snnual dinner at the Fleece Hotel, on Wednesday evening. Mr. W. J. Ashton, president of the club. presided, the vice-chairmen being Messrs. H. Galton and Nuttall. The Chairman was supported on his right ,by Messrs. S. Wolfenden, J. Hart, Beecham, and Marrow, and on his left by Messrs. Rowed (secretary), Ackerley; Whalley (ex-champion), and Nuttall. An excelleut repast was done full justice to, and the catering was in every respect satis- factory. The following is the menu :—Soups: Ox-tail, julienne. Removes : Roast beef, boiled fowls, roast turkeys

and sausages, ham, tongue, boiled leg of mution. Sweets: Pastry various, blanc mange, &c. Cheese, salad. The Cnetnistik, in proposing the "Queen and the Royal Family," referred to the assassination of the Emperor of Russia, and said there was no fear of our Queen coming to so sad a death. One of the good acts of Her Majesty had been to order tricycles in order that the limbs of the younger members of the family might be put in healthy motion, and it would be well if other families would copy her example, . .

for then tricycling would become much more popular than it was to-day. (Applause.) Mr. J. 0. Svarr proposed the "Army, navy, and reserve forces," after which Mr. Barton sung in his ustal tine style "Let me like a soldier fall." Mr.
SAMVEL WomorrpEN responded. to the toast, and

---- hurnoronsly compared the shoodng of the volunteers with that of the line, and thought the latter would do very well in giving more attention to that branch of the service. Mr. BARROW, tn proposing the toast of "The St. Helens Bicycle Club," said he was quite sine that they who were gathered there, ard who were receiving the hospitality of the club, could not withhold terms of the very warmest praise for the way in which they had been treated. But there was something more than that, which claimed their admiration arid thanks. On looking over the career of the St. Helens Bicycle Club, they could not help thinking of . . . .

the many institutions which had been formed and dissolved in tke town; but the Bicycle Club had managed to exist for a long time in an unbroken line of success. Whether on the bicycling ground, where the members had competed with other clubs, or engaged in promoting any sports in the neighbourhood, they had always been successful, and the kindly feeling that had existed amongst them, and the deter- mination to make everything successful, they could not but admire. The management generally had been good and efficient, and it would perhaps ha invidious to mention any particular names, but he should not be going beyond the bounds of propriety if he said that the success of the club was in a great measure due to their friend and fellow guest;. Mr. Rowed, the hon. secretary. (Applause.) It was net the first time he had had the honour to propose that toast, and the secretary had always given them a vety clever record of the club's performances. He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Rowed. The toast having been drunk, Mr. Hy. Grattan, described by the Chairman as the poet of the St. Helens Bicycle Club, gave a song, composed by himself, on bicycling, which was encored. Mr. ROWED, in responding to the toast, said it was cus- tomary for him to give a short notice of the doings of the club, and he would not depart from that course. At their sports Mr. Whalley won the championship, and they would remember what a very exciting contest there was between him and Mr. Mees. (Applause.) Unfortun,ttely they had a very wet afternoon for their next race in August, and he was sorry to say they lost money, and had a rather poor attendance. On that occasion Mr. Mees won a very slow and laborious race. (Applause.) They were also fortunate in having races confined to their club at the St. Helens and Sutton sports, but he was sorry they had not a better entry for the latter. Touring, he thought, had been indulged in 'mite as much as in previous years. Dr. Martin's attempt which covered 800 miles eclipsed all the others. (Ap- plause.) He was sorry they had lost Dr., Martin, because he always took a great interest in the club, and was as popular as any member they had. (Applause.) The %ecre- tary's life was not a very happy one, when he told them he forgot to write Dr. Martin until the day after Saturday. (Laughter.) He had received the reply, which said that owing to short notice he would not be able to attend. With regard to the club runs, which were those that were fixed, and at which they expected a lot of members to turn up and go out together, he was sorry to say they were falling through. But their club was not the only one, as almost all clubs made the same complaint. They, however, had had a few exceptional trips, and he was very glad to say that at the monster meet at Liverpool, as usual, they had the largest number of members present. (Applause.) They ,were not only the strongest club, but every one of their members were in club uniform. That was more than what other clubs could say who had fewer members. Mr. Beecham, the treasurer, told him that the dill) had a very substantial balance to its credit at Parr's Bank, and in order to show there was no secresy, a balance sheet would be printed in about a fortnight and a copy sent to every mem- ber of the club; and the books could be seen at any time on the Friday night's meeting. He hoped no one would think this was a smaller gathering than usual, or rather that the interest was flagging. There were 72 present; but they had not pushed the sale of tickets, thinkinc, this the next desir- able course to pursue. But at the meeting a fortnight ago there' were more members present than there had been at any previous meeting since the club started. On Saturday they unanimously resolved to change their uniform to grey, as some wanted, to be distinct from clubs who had copied them. (Applause.) The total of the club still remained at 100; he could not give the exact number, but it was not likely to decrease while their annual gatherings wereso well patrcnised. (Applause.) Glee : " Spring's delight," Messrs.Barnton, Taylor, Ander- ton, and Merrill. Mr. HOUSEMAN proposed the "Town. and trade of St. Helens," and in doing so said they could not boast very much of its beauty, but they could say it wal a very im- proving town. A friend of his said be never put his head into such a hole in his life, but unfortunately it was Novem- ber when he visited St. Helens. But besides good streets, they could ROVV show their visitors a few.good buildings, and as trade improved, he hoped those in authority would tin- prove the town ip point of beauty. It was a very good thing for the town that they had numerous trades, because when one particular business was bad there were several others which might be good. It was a grand thing to say that the town of St. Helens could hold up its head as the great centre of glass making in the world. He hoped that the prosperous times promised them so long would soon be upon them. The toast having been erunk, Mr. *John Taylor sang the "Monarch of the Woods." The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Ashton) responded to the toast, and in speaking of the manufactures of the town, said he would just like to see one more rise up, and that was the manu- facture of bicycles and tricycles. (Hear, hear.) It onlr wanted some enterprising man to commence that. He re- membered that in Coventry when bicycle making was com- menced there, people said it would scatter death all around, but it had proved a boon to that town. They had plenty of coal in St. Helens and they had foundries, and be could see no reason why people from thisdistrict, including Liver- and Manchester, should go to Coventry, and even to Lon= don for their bicycles, especially when the railway company made such heavy charges. Song : Mr. Anderton, "The Arab Steed." Mr. AMULET proposed "The neighbouring recreation clubs," remarking that he saw very few representatives of the neighbouring bicycle clubs present, but no doubt had it been some other time of the year he should have seen other representatives there. He coupled with the toast the names of Mr. Housman, Mr. West (Excelsier 8.C.), and Mr. Banks, of Sutton. The toast was cordially received, and the glee party then Sang the beautiful glee "Serenade." Mr. HOUSMAN responded on behalf of the at. Helens Cricket Club, and Mr. WEST, on behalf of the Excelsior 8.C., the latter remarking that he was not a racer, never did race, and never should do,—(A Voice: QuerY)— bit:twee admired touring, whtch he thought was the greatest feature as of bicycling. His tour did not come up to Dr. Martin's his time was limited, bat be ran over,something like 609 miles. (Applause.) Song: Three jolly sailor boys," Mr. Rowed. after which Mr. S. WOLFENDEN proposed The Visitors," rs , Mr. Barton sang" My pretty Jane," Mr. BARROW respond- ing to the toast.; The meeting closed after the singing of the National Anthem. ANOTHER EARTHQUAKE IN ITAT.Y. NAPLES, NABeR 16.—Last night another strong shock f earthquake was felt at Casamicciola, and some houses which had survived the last visitation were thrown to the ground. At Lacco Ameno and Serra Fontana the shock was also felt, and there, too, some houses fell. No one was hurt at either place.

ST. H PIENS LITERARY AND ! SCIENTIFIC -ASSOCIATION. 1 On Tuesday evening Mr. W. amble treated the memtiers of this Association to a lecture on Holland. Dr. McNicoll, in the absence of the president of the Association (Mr. R. Pilkington), presided. Mr. Warms, after a few preliminary observations, spike of one of the most important features of the country being the hydraulic works, and though a good deal was said abnut its agriculture in books treating of that country, very little was said of the hydraulic works which rendered the win- try the fertile and thriving one it now is. Owing to the floods the loss of lite had been tremendous, and yet, although Holland.was a very wet country, almost every piece of land In order to be fit for anything having to be kept well drained, the land was so light that unless water was admitted to the farms the crops would be spoilt for the lack of it. Windmills had been used iu Holland for a long time ,to raise the water, but in 1848 pumping by steam commenced at one of the large lakes, and in eleven months the level of the lake was reduced 5i inches. In 1852 the lake was dty. Although the Dutch had lone a great deal in turning the water portion of the country into land by artificial means other parts of the country had become inundated, and where three lakes had once existed separately, they were now seen as one large lake. He instanced a Case in which a man's field separated itself from the rest of his farm and floated on the water; but having secured the assistance of the administration which regulated the hydraulic works, the field was towed back to its original position. He then touched lightly upon the general appearance of the country, and the manners and customs of the people. Although they lived in a very quiet, simple manner, they had extravagances, most of I them having a fancy for plate of gold and silver, and some people actually had their kitchen utensils made of silver. Mer- chants carried on their trade in and found their markets by the canal boats; and even milk from some distant field was brought home by boat. But they must not understand that the whole of the kingdom was a reclaimed morass, as in the south they had a sandy, dry land which was mostly poor and unpromising, inhabited by strict and pious Calvinists who were remarkable for their great industry. Speaking of the manufacture of cheese in Holland, he said the time taken for its preparation was nine or ten days, and it had to be ten weeks old before it was fit for the market. For the English market the cheese was made orange colour, but for France and other countries it was made red by being rubbed with butter and rouge. The amount of cheese manufactured in North Holland per year was about 26 millions of pounds. The towns and people of Holland were scrupulously clean, and even the charwoman when going to her work looked dressed for church. One of the most remarkable things worn by the Dutch ladies was the head-dress—worn chiefly by the country people. They might not have hair like some of Dickens' heroines, who twisted theirs into a knot and fastened it up at the back; at all events, it could not be seen. It was a cap of geld or silver nearly covering the whole of the head, and was always bright and sparkling. When they wished to be even moderately dressed they put another made of lace on the top. These head-dresses cost about £9 each, and no servant girl was considered respectable without one. '

The CHAIRMAN said the bill of fare that night had been very instructive, bot there was nothing combative about the lecture, and was not one in which the ardent spirit of the gladiator or the wrestler could have much play. It was not like the mind and body question—(laughter)—or like the figure "3," which they could discuss. England had had a good deal to do with Holland in its time, and the Dutch were once considered worthy of .their (the English) steel. They seemed to have been born, well, not in a ditch—(laughter) —but certainly in an amphibious sort of condition, and he did not wonder they did dispute with the English in bygone times upon the water. He had nothing more to say, but would call upon the Rev. J. P. Ritchie. Mr. Ritchie did not rise to address the meeting, and the CHAIRMAN then moved a vote of thanks to the Lecturer for his very practical ancrinteresting lecture. Mr. A. CARR seconded the motion, and remarked that they might have been told more about the proportion of water to land in Holland. Mr. R. W. H. THOMAS supported the motion, and said he would like to have heard a little more as to the literature of the country, if they had any, and more about the chief in- dustries. There was no doubt the Dutch were a nation which had degenerated he was going to say, but rather of which they did not hear so much as formerly". In the time of Charles the Second they occupied a position amongst the countries of Europe, and fought successful battles with the British fleet. The motion having been carried, the LECTURER suitably replied, and a vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. Turmas, seconded by the Lscrtinart.

div.head: ST. HELENS PRIMITIVE METHODIST
div.p: ST. HELENS PRIMITIVE METHODIST
CHA

On Sunday, two sermons were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel by the Rev. C. Lace, of Crewe, a super annuated blind pre miler. On Monday evening the rev gentleman gave a lecture to a moderate audience, en "The great Reformation of 1683." The Rev. T. WILSHAW introduced the Mayan (Alderman Harrison), who presided, and on rising was received with applause. He thanked them very much for their reception, and said it gave him very much pleasure to be able to come and meet them on that occasion. It also gave him an oppor- tunity of showing his appreciation of the subject they had in view, that was to reduce the debt on the chapel, &c. He might also add, as Mayor of St. Helens, that he felt in an agreeable part of his duty to accede to the request of their minister. (Applause.) Referriit to the financial question, be found from a statement which had been handed to him bY their respected minister that the debt was £l,OOO, 'Plat seemed a very large sum, and he hoped that means would be adopted, as he believed there were going to be, to reduce the debt, and ultimately wipe it off altogether. It was a great burden for a small congregation, but he was sure they were all willing, and if any occasion arose he should be most happy to take part in proceedings, the object of which would be to reduce the chapel debt. (Applause.) The LECTURER, after a few, preliminary remarks, said there were bright and very, dark spots in the history of England, and one of the darkest epochs in English history was the reign of Charles IL He dared say that idea would be responded to by most ,people. Not only was the Court and the Government infected with looseness of mantiers, but the whole nation to a considerable extent affected for the worst. James 11., who succeeded Charles, was a Romanist, and exercised daring his reign a great amount of terror. It was very 'convenient far the lasciviousness of thoroughly bad men to be Romanists, as they could easily pass through purgatory, if a man could really believe in the dogmas of Romanism. Having enumerated several of the deeds of tyranny enacted during the reign of James, and spoken of the family of Stuarts as being bent upon absolutism, he went on to say that England was Protestant at that time—perhaps more so than it was to-day, and the nation was roused to action. The battle of the Boyne was fought in 1688,and then followed the downfall of Romanism; and James was compelled to take his flight. One of the first acts of William 111. was the Act of Tolera- tion, to which Methodism owed a great deal, and by which it was allowed to flourish. He enumerated several benefi- cial acts that were passed in the reign of William, amongst which were some which did away with the anomalies in English jurisprudence. William • had many enemies, for many of.the Conservatives were Jacobites who believed that kings had a sort of divine right in reigning as they liked.; but in spite of the obstacles which the Jacobites threw in the way of the king, his popularity grew and civil and religions liberty began to „make itself felt. Having compared the present with the past in regard to liberty of worship, he recited a piece of unpublished poetry written by himself, in which the deep patriotism of the lecturer was strikingly manifest. The usual votes of thanks having been given the meeting terminated. The collections at, the sermons and lecture amounted to over ;ell.

In answer to Superintendent Williamson, witness said there WAS a rule of the company to the effect that no old or other rope was permitted to be removed from the pre- mises: but it must be returned to the store.—Sergeant Walley said that, on visiting Lavelle's store, the last entry of any purchase of rope from the prisoner Bushell was on the 25th February. There was, therefore, no entry as to the purchase of the 481bs:*.of rope. Lavelle said Bushell had not been at the shop for several weeks.—P.C. Hibbert proved going to the premises of Lavelle on Saturday after- noon, and finding the stolen rope, which was covered with sacks and other things, in the back part of the place.—ln- Spector Hollingworth stated that he also visited Lavelle's store, and, on having his attention drawn to the rope, he (Lavelle) said be had examined it, but could net fin,l any- thing upon it to indicate that it was the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Co. The witness also gave a long account of his interview with-Lavelle.—On being formally charged, Bushell pleaded guilty, but Lavelle reserved his defence.—Both the prisoners were committed to the Sessions for trial, and Lavelle was admitted to bail, himself in £2O, and two sureties in £lO. TEE BOSTOCK FAMILY Aoms.—Ann Bostock was charged with assaulting Mrs. Amy Sadler, formerly Bostock, a woman well known in the police court, on the 7th bast.— Defendant is a sister-in-law of complainant, and appeared to be a very unlikely woman to commit an assaalt.—The Bench dismissed the summons, and ordered complainant to pay 3s. 4d. costs. SurroN SLAcx STRALEES. Elizabeth Harding, Emma Derlington, Betsy Foster, all elderly women, and Elizabeth Stanley, a girl, were charged with stealing 201bs. of coal, the property of Mr. Donald Lee, coal proprietor and lessee of Sutton-dock, on the 9th inst.—P.C. Speed said he was on duty at Sutton-dock, in company with P.C. Lowndes, when he saw the prisoners go to some of the wagons, and when they came away each of them had a bag of slack. He and Lowndes emptied the slack and got the names of the prisoners.—Mr. Lee said he did not wish to press the case.— Each of the prisoners was fined is. and 18s. costs, or, in de- fault, seven days' imprisonment.—ln the case of the girl Stanley, Mr. Thomas Norman and several other gentlemen, who were listening to the proceedings, subscribed the larger proportion of the fine and costs, and her friends paid the rest, on which she was set at liberty. AN INCORRIGIBLE LAD..-4VIII. H. Dunbobbin, a lad who had been previously convicted of felony, was charged with stealing 6ilbs. of pork, the property of Mr.'Samuel Crosby, provision dealer, Top Locks.—W. T. Crosby, son of the prosecutor, stated that on the previous Thursday night he saw the prisoner, who had previously caused him con- siderable trouble, loitering about the shop. He secreted himself, and. shortly after, saw the lad creep Into the shop, take the pork from a bench on which it was lying, and run away. He went after and caught him.—The Superintendent of Police said the case of the lad was a very sad one, as he seemed to be a perfect specimen of the street Arab, with rio one to care for him. He had previously been convicted of felony, and ordered to be sent to a reformatory school, but he was not put into one.—Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' cl..rk, was asked for an explanation on the subject by Mr. Bankes, and said he believed that the cause of the boy not being sent to a school was that one could not be found at the time of his committal.—The Bench committed the lad to gaol 21 days, at the end of which time he was ordered to be sent to a reformatory for five years. THIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. C. W. Hazlehurst. TEE ROPE STEALING CAss.—Peter Jackson was remanded until to-day (Saturday), on a charge of being concerned in the theft of 48Ibs of rope, the property of the Bridgewater Navigation Company, reported above.
