TheiCLEax : They always objected to do that. The Ca.stnaten (proceeding) remarked that by the com- pany not carrying out their agreement, they bad put the Board to the expense of lodging a petition, and taking the , preparatory steps for opposing their Bills in Parliament. The expenses of the Board incurred had, however, been so small, that it was not worth their while to fight the company for the difference between the expenses now incurred and the ultimate costs. The company had agreed to carry out exactly everything for which the Board asked as to Plump- ton's crossing. Unfortunately there was a small piece of land at the Appleton end at the road leading from the new bridge down to Page-lane, which had not been included in the original plane; and the company had agreed to be at half the cost of constructing this small piece of road. The expense might, possibly, amount to £l.OO. He thought he bad now noticed all the points which related to the matter of the first Bill which, it was proposed to oppose. He now movedthat the Board should oppose the Bill called No . 1 in the notice calling the meeting, and that the Clerk be empowered and instructed to take all necessary steps by petition to Parliament, or otherwise, for giving effect to such opposi- tion, for the protection of the rights and interests of the Local Board, for the district of Widnes, in relation to the object of the measure. Mr. Cams seconded the motion,',which was passed unanimously. The CHAIRMAN, in speaking of the second Bill which it was intended to oppose. said the only thing with which the Local Board appeared to be concerned in this matter 'were the feotpath crossing from Bradley to the Adelphi, and the , Lngsdale level crossing itself. By the heads of an agree- ment entered into between the company and the Board, it was provided that the former were to construct a bridge over the rails of the Bradley level crossing. As to Lugsdale, the , company had agreed to construct the road according to the plans now laid upon the table; they had also undertaken to provide the whole of the land on the south side. . ' THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, MARCH 19, 1881. • . . • WARRINGTON POLICE CASES. - MONDAY.—Before Alderman Pickmere (Mayor), Councillot Fairclough. and Mr. Z. Armitage. VAGRANCY.—John Wilson, a young man, was charged with, being an inmate of the casual ward at the Workhouse, unlawfully refusing to perform the task of work allotted to him by the master.—Mr. Curry said the prisoner entered the workhouse on Sunday night, and was provided with meat and lodging, but on Monday morning he refused to brealestones, saying he knew more about the regulations than witness did.—Prisoner said he was not able to break stones, and he would have done any other class of work.— Prisoner was committed to prison for seven days with hard labour. ASSAULT.—EIIen Preston and Margaret Mannion were summoned for assaulting Ellen Shay in Horsemarket-street, on Friday.—Complainant stated the prisoner struck her on the head and pulled her to the ground by the hair. Preston bit her finger very severely. Corroborative evidence having been given, the prisoners were each fined 10s and costs or 14 days' imprisonment. Wetaen, DAMAGE.—Thomas Shaw was charged with being drunk in Horsemarket-street on Saturday night, and also with wilfully breaking a window of the Horse Shoe Inn. He was put out of the house twice, and then broke a large window.—Prisoner was fined 10s and costs and ss. damage. S CURIOUS Dec,—Peter Duffy was charged with stealing half a cwt. of coal, value 4d, from a siding on the London and North-Western Railway, at Bank Quay, on Saturday night.—The prisoner .was seen to take the coal off' the line, and he was followed' and stopped by an inspector. —Mr. Moore, who appeared for the prisoner, pleaded in extenuation of the offence, that the prisoner was getting the coal for the benefit of the person with whom he lodged, and who was a cripple unable to work. He took it for a charitable purpose at the expensoof the railway company. —The Mayor: Curious defence that.—Mr. Moore said the prisoner had been a soldier 17 years and served in India.— The Mayor said this pilfering could not be oyerlooked„and prisoner was fined 10s. and costs. &moot A'FTENDANCE.—John Currovoy, an old man, was charged under a warrant with neglecting to send his son to school.—Mr. Riley said this was a very troublesome case. The boy's school fees had been paid by the Guardians for the last 18 months, and yet he bad only been at school 10 times for 15 months. He considered that to be robbing the Guardians.—Prisoner was fined 58. and costs. RIDING ON THE RAILWAY WITHOUT I TICKET.—George Higginbottom, a well-dressed young man, was summoned for having, on the 12th February, unlawfully travelled on ties London and North-Western Railway between Liverpool and Warrington without having previously paid his fare, and with intent to avoid payment. —Mr. Ferrand appeared for the Railway Company, and Mr. Moore defended.—Mr. Ferrand produced a free pass issued to Mr. Wildman, con- nected with the engineering department at Lime-street, Liverpool, which entitled him to travel between Lime- street, Edge Hill, and Edge Lane, and it was not transfer- able. It appeared that defendant is the brother-in-law of Mr. Wildman, and by some means on Saturday, the 12th February, he obtained possession of the pass and travelled to Warrington, where he refused to give it up until he was brought before the station master.—Mr. Moore contended that there was no intention to. avoid payment, and that de- fendant was never asked for his fare. He was a respectable young man, 19 years of age, and his father was formerly AS member of the Warrington Town Council. Many people did not look upon it as defrauding the railway company if they could travel a few extra miles without paying, and he thought it was with the intention of stopping that notion that the company were prosecuting in that caso.-I-The Mayor : The sooner it is stopped the better.—Defendant was fined 20s. and costs, or one month. ALLEGED STREET OBSTRUCTION. —John Kirwood w a summoned for obstructing Golden Grove-street, on Wed- nesday, the 9th inst., by allowing his cart to stand an un- reasonable time.—Defendant said it was net a public thoroughfare but belonged to the Ram's Head public-house, and that he had authority to tepee his cart there.—The case was adjourned until Friday for investigation. PITCH AND Toss —James Bate and Patrick Salmon, boys, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss, on Sunday, the 6th March, in Factory Yard, Latchford.—P.C. Hitch- mough produced the money he had picked up.—Mr. Hunt said the gaming which went on at that place on a Sunday was a great nuisance, and a dozen strokes with a birch rod would do the defendants good.—The boys commenced to cry, and protested they would "never do it again," and as it was the first time they had been up the case was dismissed. TUESDAY.—Bef ore Aid. Webster and Councillor Broadbent. ASSAULT ON THE Pomen.-=Thomas Hughes, carter, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Hall-street, and also with assaulthy P.C. Monaghan.—On Monday night the , officer saw the prisoner without coat in Hall-street stood I besides a man on the ground, who said the prisoner had broken his leg. The constable asked prisoner for his name, , and he said he would "serve him the same." He then , seized hold of the officer unawares, and threw him over his , head on his back, and kicked him on the legs. He was I "mad" drunk.—Mr. Hunts The other man lies in the In- firmary with his leg broken in two places—Prisoner: He ' attacked me, and being drunk, fell down and broke his leg. —Prisoner was fined 55. and costs for drunkenness, and 10s. and costs for the assault on the police. TRANSFER.—Application was made for the transfer of the license of the Royal Arms Inn, from Samuel Wakefield to Mrs. Horne, and it was granted. WEDNESDAY —Before Alderman Chandley and Councillor Fairclough. LYMM PETTY SESSIONS. FElDAY.—Before Messrs Barton, Peter Stubs, and Norris. KEEPING A DOG WITHOUT ALICENCE.—WiIIiam ChaIIDEN was charged with keeping a dog without a license.—On the 15th March P.C. Maddock visited defendant's house and asked his wife if they had a license for the dog, and she replied in the negative. They intended, she said, to make away with it, as the thought to have been poisoned. The dog was in good condition.—Defendant said his daughter had had the license in her name, and she ought to have renewed it. He could show the license that had been pre- viously taken out.—P.C. Maddock,: It's no use now; the dog is killed.—Defendant was fined 7s. Od. and costs ;

OFFENCE AGAINST THE GAME LAWS.—John Wade, a groom, was summoned for setting, on the 3rd Feb. at High Legh, a snare for the purpose of killing game, to wit, a hare.—Mr. Addenbrook appeared for the defendant, and pleaded guilty.—Walton Legh, gamekeeper for Col. Legh, High Legh, said he found three snares near the fence of Mr. Challender's garden, where defendant MRS groom, and in one of them was a hare. He watched, and in a short time defendant came, took out the hare, and carried it into the house. • Witness then asked far the hare to be delivered up, and defendant gave him it.—By Mr. Addenbrook : Defendant showed him the damage which the hares had done to the garden. He had found some snares in the same place a few mornings previous to the day in question and had knocked them down.—Mr. Addenbrook stated that the defendant was under the apprehension that 'according to the new Game Laws be was eatitled to snare rabbits and be did not intend to catch hares. He asked them to inflict a small penalty under those circumstances.—Witness stated, in answer to the Chairman, that defendant was discharged from his em- ployment for that offence.—The Bench thought the law would be satisfied if defendant paid casts, 115. " BREACH OF THE EDUCATION Acr.—Peter navenscroft, who did not appear, was summoned for not sendiag his children, Charles (11) and George 49), to school.—Mr. Toft, school attendance officer, said the case had been adjourned from November last and since that time Charles had made 45 attendances and George 31 out of a possible 135. The School Attendance Committee applied for them to be sent to the Industrial School at Stockport. The Guardians had agreed to pay the expenses, Sc. monthly. The chiloiren were Protestants.—The Bench made the order as requested , until the children were sixteen.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A WATCH.—Joseph Wilkinson, cow- man, was charged with stealing a watch, valne.£l 10s., the property of John Rogers, carter.—lt appeared that the pro- secutor and the prisoner both lived at the farm of Joseph Dawson, Dunham Massey, and that on Tuesday, the 15th inst., they were drinking together at the Axe and Cleaver beerhouse, Dunham Massey. Prosecutor arrived home alone about eleven o'clock, but being unable to obtain admission into the house, he laid himself down in the shippon, putting his watch into his hat, which he deposited in a corner, and covered it with straw. He awoke in the middle of the night and on feeling for his watch to ascertain the time, found it had gone. Prisoner was then laid beside him. Proseeutor searched for his watch but was unable to find it.—P.C. Poole apprehended the prisoner at Mrs. Hogan's beerhouse, Dtmham, on the following day. He then had the watch in his pocket, and stared he had found it on the milking stool in the shippon. He was very drunk.—Sergeant Harring- ton said prisoner had made a statement to him that morning that he bad some years ago been sent to gaol for 21 days for stealing a watch on the railway, at Dunham Massey.—Pri- soner stated that whilst on his way to Dunham, the follow- ing day, he pulled the watch out of his pocket with his handkerchief, and he had expressed his intention of re- turning the watch.—Prisoner was committed for trial to Knutsford Sessions. MASTER AND SERVANT CASE—Peter John Jackson, fustian cutter, was summoned, being the servant of Mary and Fredk. Moston, for having en the 28th Dec., left their service, whereby they sustained damage and loss to the extent of £2 15s. 6d.—Mr. Addenbrooke defended, and objected to the summons on the ground that the particulars of the claim were not annexed, which was required according to the rules.—The Magistrates' Clerk said it was simply a technical objection and he considered the particulars to be sefficiently stated on the summons to enable them to defend it.--Mr Addenbrooke waived the objection.-An agreement dated September 25th, 1880, was put in in which defendant agreed to work for the complainants at the list prices and not to leave their service without giving a month's notice.—Frederick Moston said that on December 24th, defendant had had advanced for work to be done £2 ss. 6d. On Wednesday December 22nd, defendant took out a piece of work which would take him three days to cut, but he left on the 29th of , that month, when he had only cut half of it. Witness gave a lentby explanation of the rules in force at his workshop, and said defendant on the sth February, offered to pay the money claimed by instahnents of 4s. per month.—By Mr. Stubs: He hired and paid a woman to finish the piece which defendant left unfinished.—Henry Moston gave evidence as to defendant taking the piece on the understanding that he was to com- plete it.—Mr. Addenbrook, in the course of his remarks, said defendant left because complainants would not give him piece of work to which he was entitled according to the rules of the shop.—Defendant was sworn, and stated that he did not undertake to finish the piece, but only one side of it. He admitted £1 15s. Ga. of the claim. .He had not re- ceived the money for work to be done but as a loan. He received Os. 2d. for the work be was to do on the piece. He understood when be signed the agreement that he was to do a certain class of work and be left because they did not supply him with it —The Chairman said the Bench con- sidered the agreement very one sided, and that some clear rules ought to be adopted by the trade and put in the work- shops. Defendant had been under a wrong impression, but they thought he had no dishonest intention.—Mr. Moston signified his willingness to accept 6s. per month, and de- fendant was ordered to pay the claim at that rate.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, TAMIL On Sunday evening sermons were preached in the above place of worship by the Rev. J. Graham of Birkenhead, to large congregations. The collections, which realised a handsome sum, were in aid of the Foreign Missions. On Wednesday evening a public meeting was held to still further advocate the claims of the Foreign Missions. Mr. P. Warburton oc- cupied the chair and gave an address. Addresses were also given by the Revs. J. Graham, S. Stafford, and J. Thoma- son. The collection altogether realised £l2, to which amount Miss Thomason collected a very good sum. Votes of thanks to the Chairman and speakers concluded the meeting.

div.head: WEST WIDNES RAILWAY.
div.p: THE WEST WIDNES RAILWAY.

Vice-Chancellor Bristowe, sitting at his chambers in Old Square, Lincoln's Inn, made an interim order on Monday restraining the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire and Midland Railways' Joint Committee from constructing that part of the West Widnes Railway which crossed the Old Bank Farm at Ditton otherwise than according to the plans agreed to in 1878. The application was made ex-pane by the trustees of Colonel Blundell, the tenant for life of the property, with whom an agreement had been come to by the predecessor in title of the Joint Committee for the construc- tion of a branch line to his stone quarries. He alleged ithat the defendants wereTdeparting from the original plans n a 'manner injurious to his interests, and the Vice-Chancellor granted an injunction for a week upon the plaintiffs under- taking to be answerable in damages.

The Pub- lishers, in submitting the Prospectus of the Fourth Edition of the Directory of this County, respectfully hope for a con- tinuance of the patronage of their former Subscribers. The work will contain a topographical account of each Parish, Village, Hamlet. and Township, with its distance from London and other (thief towns, its position in the division of the County, Hundred and Union, and County Court District, and also the Diocese, Arehdeacoury and Rural Deanery; Des- oription of the Churches, with the Value of the Living, and the names of the Patron 'aril Incumbent, the chief Landowners; the Acreage, notice of Soil and Crops, Local Markt-a, and des- cription of the Principal Seats. In the towns are also given a Short historical account, paiticulars of the Local Government: an Architectural Description of the Churches and other Public: Buildings, chapeLs of different DenomMations; Public Schools, a full account of the Principal Manufacturies of which each town is the seat; the Markets, Fairs, and Paces; AgricultmaL and Scientific Societies and Meetings, Ac.; Objects of Natural Curiosity and Antiquities; Hospitals, Almshouses and Charities. The Directory of each town comprises Lists of the Resident Nobility, Clergy, and Gentry, and also a list of all engaged in Professional and Mercantile Pursuits, In Alphabetical Order. Information relating to Law and Public Offices, Churches and Chapels, the arrival and departure of the Mails and Coaches, Posting Houses, Commercial inns, together with particulars respecting Conveyance by Railway, lA ater or Land Carriers. will also be included. Immediately following will be given an Alphabetical Arrangement of Names of the Nobihty, Clergy, and Gentry, and a General Cachification of Trades, which will exhibit all the Persons engaged in any Trade throughout the County. 266.—Sanumav--Santanurrol. It is supposed by some to be a famous scold's name of former times, bad in remembrance for the benefit of us in these days. One authority says it is derived from the skimming ladle used for beating the victim. It is the name applied to the procession in honour of a man who has been beaten by his wife. The neighbours assemble around with a miscellaneous assortment of ladles, cleavers, bones, frying pans, and such like, at the man's abode, and either took him, or his next neighbour consented to go in his stead, be- hind a woman on horse back, he riding with his face to the horse's tail. Thus was he treated for being so disgraced by his partner. T., Winsford. c.-- 207.—" GRINNING LINE A CHESHIRE CAT." Cheese was formerly sold in Cheshire moulded in the form of a cat. The allusion is to the grinning cheese cat, but it is applied to persons who show their teeth and gums when they laugh. DATID. This phrase appears to owe its origin to the unhappy attempts of a sign-painter resident in Cheshire to represent a lion rampart—which was the crest of an influential family —on the signboards of many of the inns. The resemblance of those lions to cats caused them generally to be designated by the humbler name. A similar instance is to be found in the village of Charlton, between Pewsev and Devizes, Wilt- shire. A public-house by the roadside is commonly known by the name of "The Cat at Charlton." The sign of the house was originally a lion or tiger or some such animal the crest of the family of Sir Edward Poore. J. T. 208.—" THE GRIFFIN." The Griffin is an imaginary monstre of antiquity, commonly represented with the body, feet, and claws of a lion, the head and wings of an eagle, and instead of a mane, a comb of fishes fins. According to tradition it is repre- sented to be larger than an eagle, and that it was master of all beasts except the lion and elephant. It has the claws of an eagle on its fore feet, and those of a lion on its bind feet. The name Griffin is bestowed upon a kind of bird that is found in Siberia, also called to Tawny Vulture. Warrington. T. G. Gaon/um. 269.—REBEcravrEs. This name was applied to the Welsh, who, as in Laban and Bethnal's prayer for Rebecca's children that they might "possess the gates of those which hate gem," wished to possess the toll gates, which in 1839 were increasing so fast as to be intolerable to the Welsh. The riots to pull them up and destroy them caused Government to interfere; but as the grievance was proved real, and remedied, the Rebecca- ites gave up riots. .1., Winsford.
